answers.text:
Part 1: Whether Tax Court found an Arabian horse breeding and showing operation to be a hobby rather than a business

The Tax Court has found Arabian horse breeding and showing operations to be engaged in for profit (business) rather than as hobbies in most cases before it, but has also found such an operation to be a hobby in at least one case.

**Cases finding business purpose (not hobby):**

In *Gutierrez-Chapin*, the Tax Court found that taxpayers "pursued horse breeding as a business rather than a hobby and have established, by a preponderance of the evidence, that their primary objective was to make a profit," noting they "devoted substantial time and effort to horse breeding" and "performed all aspects of the work themselves" in what was "arduous daily work." [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

In *Helmick*, the Tax Court concluded that the taxpayers' activities indicated "they had the requisite profit objective," particularly because the Helmicks pursued a 9-year lawsuit to obtain clear title to a stallion specifically to increase profits and enable registration and sale of horses as registered purebreds. [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25]

In *Dennis*, the Court found that the taxpayer's "studied the business aspect of the horse breeding activity and developed a plan" and "took each calculated step" to actuate his business model, and this "factor supports a finding that petitioners had a profit objective." [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27]

**Case finding mixed or unfavorable result:**

In *Himmel*, the Tax Court found that petitioners did not credibly consult with experts in a manner indicating profit objective and that their experience did not demonstrate requisite financial expertise in the Arabian horse industry. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *17-18]

In *Betts*, the Court noted the activity "had considerable personal and recreational aspects" and that the taxpayer "received considerable enjoyment from riding, owning, and competing with horses," though the opinion does not provide a final determination. [T.C. Memo. 2010-164, at *19-21]

Part 1: Has the Tax Court found an Arabian horse breeding and showing operation to be a hobby rather than a business?

The Tax Court has found Arabian horse breeding and showing operations to be **businesses rather than hobbies** in the cases presented.

In *Sydney L. Gutierrez-Chapin v. Commissioner*, the court concluded that "Petitioners pursued horse breeding as a business rather than a hobby and have established, by a preponderance of the evidence, that their primary objective was to make a profit." [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

Commissioner*, the court concluded that the manner in which the activity was conducted, including a 9-year lawsuit to obtain clear title to a stallion (motivated by profit rather than pleasure), indicated "that they had the requisite profit objective." [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25]

However, in *Mark P. Himmel & Deborah W. Himmel v. Commissioner*, the Tax Court's opinion does not explicitly state the final determination on hobby versus business status in the excerpts provided. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35]

The determination in each case depends on evaluating all facts and circumstances, including time and effort devoted, expertise, manner of conducting the activity, and personal motives, under *Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b)*. [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

answers.text:
Based on the sources provided, the Tax Court has **not** found an Arabian horse breeding and showing operation to be a hobby rather than a business in the cases cited.

In fact, the Tax Court reached the opposite conclusion in the cases where it made determinations on the merits:

- In **Gutierrez-Chapin**, the Court found that "Petitioners pursued horse breeding as a business rather than a hobby and have established, by a preponderance of the evidence, that their primary objective was to make a profit." [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

- In **Helmick**, the Court concluded that "the manner in which the activity is conducted" indicated "that they had the requisite profit objective." [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25]

- In **Dennis**, the Court found that "This factor supports a finding that petitioners had a profit objective." [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27]

Expertise of Petitioners or Their Advisors
A taxpayer’s own expertise, research, and extensive study of an activity, or consultation with experts may indicate a profit objective. Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b)(2). This factor focuses on whether the taxpayer “received advice from the experts as to the accepted principles and economics of profitably running a business and not merely the general advice that a horse enthusiast would seek in training and showing horses as a hobby.” Betts, T.C. Memo. 2010-164, slip op. at 19 (and cases cited thereat).
Petitioners did not employ any specialized workers to help manage the ranch. Their only employees were students that attended the local university that were hired seasonally in the 1980s, drivers that were hired occasionally to haul trucks and set up at horse shows in the 1990s, and a limited number of part-time people throughout the years at issue.
Petitioners contend that they consulted with two individuals with extensive experience with Arabian horse operations, Mr. Dearth and Mr. Gangi; however, petitioners did not produce evidence that credibly demonstrates they received any advice that was not merely general advice a horse enthusiast would seek for a hobby. Petitioners never hired Mr. Dearth or Mr. Gangi as a professional consultant. Moreover, Mr. Dearth did not meet petitioners until 1991—a decade after Plantation Arabians was established. petitioners consulted with experts in a manner that indicates a profit objective.

**Tax year: 2026**

No. A social media influencer cannot deduct cable and streaming subscriptions as business expenses.

Payments for cable and streaming subscriptions are not deductible business expenses if they are not directly related to the taxpayer's business. [26 CFR 1.274-2(c)(1)] Viewing television and online videos is a common source of personal enjoyment, and such payments are personal expenses rather than business expenses. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15]

Even if an expense is typical for influencers, it remains non-deductible under section 162(a) if not incurred primarily for business purposes. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *18-19] An expense is deductible under section 162(a) only if it is primarily undertaken for business, instead of personal, purposes. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *16-17]

To substantiate the amounts Mr. Sami points to lines in his bank and credit card statements which show regular monthly charges of about $100 to $200 for DirectTV, $90 for TimeWarner (later replaced by $90 for Spectrum), and $10 regular payments to WWE and Apple. Starting in 2020 he also claimed deductions for subscription payments to Netflix and Hulu.
Viewing television and online videos is a common source of personal enjoyment, and we are not convinced from Mr. Sami’s testimony that these payments were directly related to his business. See, e.g., Minick v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2010-12, 99 T.C.M. (CCH) 1054, 1057 (“Payments for television and cable bills are not deductible business expenses if they were not directly related to a taxpayer’s business.” (Emphasis added.)). Consequently, we hold that these are personal expenses that Mr. Sami is not entitled to deduct.

Mr. Sami did not keep records or provide other evidence of the split between business use and personal use of his four cell phones. Clearly some was business use, as it would have been essential to his providing transportation services, which involved calls to schedule pickups and GPS to navigate while driving. For example, four different phones and cell services seem excessive for a business run by Mr. Sami outside his regular full-time employment.
While Mr. Sami did not provide the exact amount of business versus personal use, some business use was clearly incurred. Consequently, we will estimate under the Cohan rule. See, e.g., Hoakison v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2022-117, at *28–29 (applying the Cohan rule to estimate phone expenses). We likewise note that we “bear[] heavily . . . upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making” by failing to maintain contemporaneous business records. Cohan v. a business perspective to have at least one of the four phones, we will allow Mr. Sami to deduct 25% of his reported expenses for cell phone service.

Television and Video Streaming
Mr. Sami claimed deductions of $2,896, $3,211, and $3,766 for television and video streaming expenses for tax years 2019, 2020, and 2021, respectively, under the label of “market research.” He argues that the expenses were for business purposes because they allowed him to learn about entertainment events, to which he could then sell tickets, and trends that might help him in his social media influencer activities.

Mr. Sami also argues that these expenses are usual, and so ordinary, expenses for influencers. Disney-focused influencers, for example, pay to go to film premieres, Mr. Sami says, so they can then post videos and images of the premieres and generate income. This may be, but even if Mr. Sami’s expenses are typical influencer expenses, they are still not deductible under section 162(a), since they were not incurred primarily for business purposes.
Even if Mr. Sami had incurred these expenses primarily for business purposes, there are further problems, which fall broadly into two buckets: first, whether, if the facts are as Mr. Sami states, he has met the other legal requirements for these deductions; second, whether Mr. Sami has substantiated that the facts are as he states.
As for the first set of problems, Mr. Sami did not receive payments from social media companies during the tax years at issue. Further, his celebrity interactions did not materially benefit his driving business, since, without a TLC license, he could drive only individuals he
personally knew. And he has not shown that these marketing expenses increased his ticket sale business, since he provided no written evidence of any ticket sales. Consequently, the most promising way these could be business expenses is if they were early costs for his socialmedia-revenue-sharing line of business. However, that line of business, even if now producing fruit, was not at the time—making such expenses more likely startup expenditures that must be capitalized under section 195. This would require much more legal analysis than Mr. Sami has proffered.

We come now to the main event.
Expenses are deductible under section 162(a) only if they are primarily undertaken for business, instead of personal, purposes. Walliser v. Commissioner, 72 T.C. 433, 437–38 (1979). In the textbookfavorite Danville Plywood, for example, employees of a plywood manufacturing company went on a weekend trip to the Super Bowl with some customers, and the company reported the employees’ expenses as business expenses. Danville Plywood Corp. v. United States, 899 F.2d 3, 5–6 (Fed. Cir. 1990). The court held that the employees’ expenses were not deductible under section 162(a), since the trip was “a group social excursion with business playing a subsidiary role.” Danville Plywood, 899 F.2d at 9. By contrast, in Tucker, a struggling fashion label entrepreneur appeared on a local public television show with models wearing the label’s clothes. Tucker v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo.
2023-87, at *4–5, aff’d, No. 24-1147, 2025 WL 511651 (1st Cir. Jan. 6, 2025). We held that, under section 162(a), the entrepreneur could deduct the expenses for this appearance, since the entrepreneur’s “primary motive or purpose in appearing on the show was to increase [the label’s] visibility and in turn generate sales of [its] products.” Tucker, T.C. Memo. 2023-87, at *14.
The Court has not had the opportunity to apply these general principles in the context of expenses incurred by social media influencers; however, such an enterprise would be no different from other for-profit enterprises, and the same general rules would apply.

**2026**

INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.

The sources do not provide definitive guidance for 2026. The most directly applicable authority is [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15], which holds that cable and streaming subscription payments are not deductible business expenses where they are not "directly related to a taxpayer's business" and viewing is "a common source of personal enjoyment." That case involved a social media influencer who claimed cable and streaming deductions as "market research" but could not establish the expenses were incurred primarily for business rather than personal purposes.

However, the sources do not answer whether a different factual showing—such as evidence that subscriptions were directly related to the active conduct of the influencer business, or that the expenses were primarily undertaken for business purposes—would permit a deduction. The regulation [26 CFR 1.274-2(c)(1)] requires that entertainment expenses be "directly related to the active conduct" of business, but does not clarify how that standard applies to subscription services used for content research or trend analysis by influencers.

To answer your question, I would need sources addressing: (1) what constitutes "direct relation" to an influencer's business; (2) whether subscriptions used to research content, audience trends, or entertainment topics satisfy that standard; or (3) IRS guidance specific to influencer business expenses.

a business perspective to have at least one of the four phones, we will allow Mr. Sami to deduct 25% of his reported expenses for cell phone service.
However, we have no basis for determining that the purported charges for cell phone equipment were for business rather than personal use and will not allow deductions for those reported expenses.
C.
Television and Video Streaming
Mr. Sami claimed deductions of $2,896, $3,211, and $3,766 for television and video streaming expenses for tax years 2019, 2020, and 2021, respectively, under the label of “market research.” He argues that the expenses were for business purposes because they allowed him to learn about entertainment events, to which he could then sell tickets, and trends that might help him in his social media influencer activities.

contexts.text:
Mr. Sami also argues that these expenses are usual, and so ordinary, expenses for influencers. Disney-focused influencers, for example, pay to go to film premieres, Mr. Sami says, so they can then post videos and images of the premieres and generate income. This may be, but even if Mr. Sami’s expenses are typical influencer expenses, they are still not deductible under section 162(a), since they were not incurred primarily for business purposes.
Even if Mr. Sami had incurred these expenses primarily for business purposes, there are further problems, which fall broadly into two buckets: first, whether, if the facts are as Mr. Sami states, he has met the other legal requirements for these deductions; second, whether Mr. Sami has substantiated that the facts are as he states.
As for the first set of problems, Mr. Sami did not receive payments from social media companies during the tax years at issue. Further, his celebrity interactions did not materially benefit his driving business, since, without a TLC license, he could drive only individuals he
personally knew. And he has not shown that these marketing expenses increased his ticket sale business, since he provided no written evidence of any ticket sales. Consequently, the most promising way these could be business expenses is if they were early costs for his socialmedia-revenue-sharing line of business. However, that line of business, even if now producing fruit, was not at the time—making such expenses more likely startup expenditures that must be capitalized under section 195. This would require much more legal analysis than Mr. Sami has proffered.

Expenses are deductible under section 162(a) only if they are primarily undertaken for business, instead of personal, purposes. Walliser v. Commissioner, 72 T.C. 433, 437–38 (1979). answers.question: Can a social media influencer deduct cable and streaming subscriptions as business expenses?

answers.text:
**2026**

Part 2: Deductibility of cable and streaming subscriptions for social media influencers

No. A social media influencer cannot deduct cable and streaming subscriptions as business expenses.

Viewing television and online videos is a common source of personal enjoyment, and payments for television and cable bills are not deductible business expenses if they were not directly related to the taxpayer's business. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15] In the case of a social media influencer who claimed deductions for DirectTV, TimeWarner, Spectrum, WWE, Apple, Netflix, and Hulu subscriptions as "market research," the Tax Court held that these were personal expenses not entitled to deduction because the taxpayer did not establish they were directly related to the business. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15]

This conclusion applies even if such expenses are typical for influencers, because expenses are deductible under section 162(a) only if they are primarily undertaken for business rather than personal purposes. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *16-17] The same general rules applicable to other for-profit enterprises apply to social media influencer enterprises. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *17]

See, e.g., Minick v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2010-12, 99 T.C.M. Consequently, we hold that these are personal expenses that Mr. Sami is not entitled to deduct.

As with other expenses he has reported, the bank and credit card statements merely have lines with a date, a payment amount, and a “description” that is less than helpful. For example, the description of the first general marketing payment of 2019 is “Idigic” followed by a string of 34 numerals.

# 2026 Tax Year

INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.

The sources provided address the Tax Court's treatment of **farm workers' employment classification** when given housing, insurance, and pay advances, but they do not directly answer how the Tax Court has treated the **farm workers themselves** for tax purposes (e.g., their income inclusion, deduction treatment, or reporting obligations).

What the sources do establish:

The Tax Court has held that when a farm provides workers with housing, insurance coverage, and pay advances—along with other indicia of control—this supports classifying those workers as **employees rather than independent contractors** for employment tax purposes. [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13] Specifically, the Court found that a farm's provision of workers' compensation and employer's liability insurance, coverage of job-related expenses, provision of on-site housing, and allowance of wage advances were "far more indicative of an intention to create an employment relationship than they are of an intention to create an independent-contractor relationship." [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13]

However, the sources do not address:
- How the workers' receipt of housing should be treated for their own tax purposes
- Whether advance payments create income or deferred compensation treatment
- Any other tax consequences specific to the workers themselves

As with other disallowed deductions relating to the machine shed, respondent disallowed the insurance payments on the basis that petitioners’ tractors were personal expenditures, rather than business expenses. Having found supra that the tractors were purchased for and used in petitioners’ farm operation, the Court holds the payments for insurance on the machine shed were appropriately claimed as business expense deductions.
Respondent determined that petitioners’ umbrella insurance policy payments were nondeductible personal expenses because the policy covered all potential liability, regardless of whether personal or business, and the $1 million amount covered more than their regular home policy. Petitioners argue that the coverage extended beyond home coverage and that they purchased the insurance to protect against farm catastrophes. Petitioners maintain a farming operation that includes over 400 acres of land, heavy machinery, and a cattle herd of over 30 head of cattle, and maintaining an insurance policy to protect against potential liability is a common business expense. Because the insurance covered both personal and business liability, however, the Court must allocate the expense. The size and value of the farming operation far exceeding that of petitioners’ home (which was already covered by petitioners’ homeowners insurance policy), the Court concludes that 75% of the umbrella policy premiums were business-related expenses.
The Court holds that petitioners are entitled to Schedule F deductions for insurance (other than health) of $560.75, $597.75, and $713.75 above the amounts respondent allowed in the notice or otherwise conceded.

Here, the workers were employed by petitioner throughout the years at
issue. Furthermore, the workers actually maintained their primary residence on
petitioner's property in a trailer provided to them by petitioner. Although there is
no evidence of a contractual arrangement between petitioner and the workers
creating an explicit permanent employment relationship, the relationship in
practice was certainly ongoing. Because the workers were long-term employees
who actually resided on the farm, it cannot be said that the relationship was
transitory or temporary. Therefore, we find that this factor is also supportive of an
employer-employee relationship.
7. Relationship the Parties Thought They Created
Petitioner contends that the relationship created by the parties was intended
to be that of a business and independent contractors. However, the relationship
between petitioner and the workers does not support such a characterization. The
record indicates that petitioner purchased workers' compensation and employer's
liability insurance for the years at issue.
In addition, petitioner covered all of the
job-related expenses necessary for the workers to perform their duties. Petitioner
even provided a residence on the property for the workers and allowed the workers
to receive advances on their compensation. These actions are far more indicative
of an intention to create an employment relationship than they are of an intention
to create an independent-contractor relationship. Therefore, this factor also
supports the existence of an employer-employee relationship.
On the basis of a careful consideration of the foregoing factors, in the light
of the facts and circumstances particular to this case, we hold that the workers
were petitioner's employees for purposes of Federal employment taxes during the
years at issue.

Petitioner was formed on October 11, 2005. From January 1, 2006, to
December 31, 2008 (years at issue), petitioner's primary activity was the
raising, inventorying, training, marketing, and showing of horses for anticipated
sales, and/or anticipated prospective use for lessons and/or leasing of horses.
Petitioner's sole owner and sole corporate officer was Diana Militana. Diana
Militana has been involved in the equestrian business at other locations and with
other entities. Diana Militana is married to Richard Militana.
During the years at issue at least six horses were, for at least some time, kept
on property which petitioner had the right to occupy. The property on which
petitioner operates consists of approximately 114 acres and includes woods, a
meadow, a barn with a tack room, a metal corral, a house (in which the Militanas
lived), a trailer, cross fencing, and a fence surrounding the property. The house on
the property includes a stable office (which the Militanas used to work on
equestrian-related business) and is surrounded by grounds on which horses can be
displayed and observed from either the office or the front porch.
During 2006 and continuing through 2007 and 2008 petitioner engaged two
farm workers, Adam Lopez Morales and Nallhelyo Ruiz (workers), to work on the
property. The workers lived in the trailer on the property and do not appear to
ever have paid rent. For the years at issue petitioner purchased workers'
compensation and employer's liability insurance from American National Property
and Casualty.
During the years at issue the workers' job duties included: cleaning stalls,
the barn area, the barn offices, the rest room, and the tack room; grooming horses;
watering the horses; and moving the horses between pastures. The harnesses,
brushes and combs, shovels, pitchforks, wheelbarrow, manure spreader, and
brooms used to care for the horses and barn were all owned by petitioner.

With respect to the payments to Farmers Mutual, petitioners introduced into evidence pages from a 2015 invoice showing $1,492 due and bank records showing payment of the invoice. The invoice lists several vehicles and other equipment covered by the policy, but petitioners have not introduced any additional evidence connecting those items with the farming operation or, in the case of the vehicles, have not satisfied the requirements of section 274(d). On the basis of the invoice and petitioners’ other records, the Court will allow an additional deduction of $36, representing the premiums paid for equipment designated on the invoice as “Farm Use Only.” The remaining amounts paid to EMC and Farmers Mutual are disallowed.
The remaining vehicle expenses relate to items charged on petitioners’ Discover credit card, the bulk of which were at Casey’s General Store in Creston, Iowa. Petitioners argue that these amounts represented fuel and other purchases related to their vehicles. However, they did not introduce receipts or other evidence demonstrating what those charges represent or allocating the fuel purchases among their personal and business vehicles. Although Mrs. Hoakison documented the purchases in her ledger, the ledgers do not provide sufficient detail to allow the Court a basis for allocation.
Finally, respondent disallowed petitioners’ claimed deductions of $57, $93, and $155 for the cost of magazine subscriptions to Farm Show in 2013, Ageless Iron Almanac and Farm Show in 2014, and Farm Show, Farm Collector, and Ageless Iron Almanac in 2015, respectively. Mr. Hoakison testified that he used the magazines for information about farming, tractors, and tractor maintenance. On review of the evidence, the Court will allow deductions of $50 and $20 for 2014 and 2015, respectively, for the cost of Ageless Iron Almanac. The Court finds that petitioners have not sufficiently demonstrated that the remaining amounts were not personal expenses and will disallow the deductions.

Pursuant to the 2007 oral agreement, LHDC provided Louisiana Assisted services (through its workers, both workers treated as employees and workers treated as independent contractors), office space, and information systems, to assist Louisiana Assisted in administering the Mississippi Gulf Coast DHAP program. LHDC also administered its own contracts.

answers.question: How has the Tax Court treated farm workers who were given housing, insurance and pay advances by the farm?

answers.text:
# Tax Court Treatment of Farm Workers with Housing, Insurance, and Pay Advances

Based on the sources provided, the Tax Court has treated such arrangements as indicative of an **employer-employee relationship** rather than independent contractor status.

In *Twin Rivers Farm, Inc. v. Commissioner*, the Tax Court examined a farm operation where workers were provided housing (a trailer on the property), employer's liability insurance, and advances on their compensation. [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *3-4]

The Court found that several factors supported employee status:

**Housing and Long-Term Residence:**
The workers "actually maintained their primary residence on petitioner's property in a trailer provided to them by petitioner" and the "relationship in practice was certainly ongoing," so it could not be characterized as "transitory or temporary." [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13]

**Insurance and Expense Coverage:**
The fact that "petitioner purchased workers' compensation and employer's liability insurance for the years at issue" and "covered all of the job-related expenses necessary for the workers to perform their duties" demonstrated an intention to create an employment relationship. [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13]

**Pay Advances:**
The provision that workers "could receive advances on their compensation" was cited as evidence "far more indicative of an intention to create an employment relationship than they are of an intention to create an independent-contractor relationship." [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13]

The Court ultimately concluded that the workers were employees for federal employment tax purposes. [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13]

# Part 1: Toll and Parking Charges on a Spreadsheet

No. A spreadsheet of toll and parking charges alone is insufficient to substantiate travel expenses.

In *Simpson v. Commissioner*, the Tax Court rejected a taxpayer's spreadsheet listing toll tag charges and parking fees because: (1) the expenses did not clearly correspond with the travel destinations on the taxpayer's travel logs, and (2) the taxpayer's testimony at trial did not corroborate the assertions in the travel logs. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19] The court held that the spreadsheet "lacks the specificity and detail required under Temporary Treasury Regulation § 1.274-5T(c)(3)(i)(A)." [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19]

Under section 274(d), travel expenses require substantiation of four elements: (1) the amount of each expenditure, (2) the date of departure and return and number of business days, (3) the destination or locality of travel, and (4) the business reason for travel. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *18] Each element must be supported by "adequate records" or "sufficient evidence corroborating the taxpayer's own statement." [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *18]

A mere spreadsheet listing small expenses without clear connection to documented travel destinations and without contemporaneous or corroborating testimony fails to meet these heightened substantiation requirements.

With respect to petitioners’ travel expenses for taxable year 2011, petitioners’ position at trial was that Getify was entitled to deduct $5,954. Respondent’s position at trial was that Getify was entitled to deduct $4,456, which flows through to petitioners’ Schedule E. Also, respondent averred that petitioners were entitled to deduct $1,034 as unreimbursed employee expenses, which falls under the category of “miscellaneous itemized deductions,” is subject to the two-percent limitation under section 67(a), and is reportable on petitioners’ Schedule A. By this, respondent signals that petitioners have sufficiently substantiated $5,490 worth of travel expenses for 2011. Accordingly, the parties dispute whether the discrepancy of $464 has been properly substantiated.
Travel expenses are subject to heightened substantiation requirements under section 274(d). Those requirements permit a deduction for traveling expenses only to the extent the taxpayer proves (1) the amount of each expenditure for traveling away from home, (2) the date of departure and return for each trip and the number of days spent on business, (3) the destination or locality of travel, and (4) the business reason for travel or the expected business benefit to be derived. See Temp. Treas. Reg. § 1.274-5T(b)(2). Each element of a traveling expense must be substantiated through “adequate records” or by “sufficient evidence corroborating the taxpayer’s own statement.” See § 274(d)
(flush language); see also Temp. Treas. Reg. § 1.274-5T(c)(1), (2), and (3).
Petitioners provided a spreadsheet of their 2011 travel expenses. The disputed expenses involve numerous small amounts associated with toll tag charges and parking fees. These expenses do not clearly correspond with the travel destinations on petitioners’ travel logs. Moreover, when asked about several of these expenses at trial, Mr. Simpson did not provide testimony that corroborated the assertions made in petitioners’ travel logs.

# Answer

No. Toll and parking charges on a spreadsheet alone are not enough to substantiate travel expenses.

In *Kyle D. Simpson & Christen Simpson v. Commissioner*, the taxpayers provided a spreadsheet of 2011 travel expenses that included "numerous small amounts associated with toll tag charges and parking fees." Memo. 2023-4, at *19] The Court found that the "disputed spreadsheet items lack[ed] the specificity and detail required" and that the taxpayer's testimony did not corroborate the assertions in the travel logs. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19]

[T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *18] A spreadsheet listing toll and parking charges without clear correspondence to travel destinations and without corroborating testimony fails to meet these requirements.

answers.question: Are toll and parking charges on a spreadsheet enough to substantiate travel expenses?

answers.text:
# Answer

No. Toll and parking charges on a spreadsheet alone are insufficient to substantiate travel expenses.

In *Kyle D. Simpson & Christen Simpson v. Commissioner*, taxpayers provided a spreadsheet of 2011 travel expenses including toll tag charges and parking fees. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19] The court held that the spreadsheet "lacks the specificity and detail required under Temporary Treasury Regulation § 1.274-5T(c)(3)(i)(A)" and that the taxpayers "failed to satisfy their burden of substantiating" the expenses. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19] The problem was that the disputed expenses did not "clearly correspond with the travel destinations on petitioners' travel logs" and the taxpayer's trial testimony did not corroborate the assertions in the logs. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19]

Travel expenses require substantiation of four elements: "(1) the amount of each expenditure for traveling away from home, (2) the date of departure and return for each trip and the number of days spent on business, (3) the destination or locality of travel, and (4) the business reason for travel." [T.C. Memo. 2023-26, at *5] Substantiation requires either "adequate records" or "sufficient evidence corroborating the taxpayer's own statement." [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *18-19]

A spreadsheet of tolls and parking lacks the contemporaneous detail and clear connection to travel destinations necessary to meet these requirements.

contexts.text:
With respect to petitioners’ travel expenses for taxable year 2011, petitioners’ position at trial was that Getify was entitled to deduct $5,954. Respondent’s position at trial was that Getify was entitled to deduct $4,456, which flows through to petitioners’ Schedule E. Also, respondent averred that petitioners were entitled to deduct $1,034 as unreimbursed employee expenses, which falls under the category of “miscellaneous itemized deductions,” is subject to the two-percent limitation under section 67(a), and is reportable on petitioners’ Schedule A. By this, respondent signals that petitioners have sufficiently substantiated $5,490 worth of travel expenses for 2011. Accordingly, the parties dispute whether the discrepancy of $464 has been properly substantiated.
Travel expenses are subject to heightened substantiation requirements under section 274(d). Those requirements permit a deduction for traveling expenses only to the extent the taxpayer proves (1) the amount of each expenditure for traveling away from home, (2) the date of departure and return for each trip and the number of days spent on business, (3) the destination or locality of travel, and (4) the business reason for travel or the expected business benefit to be derived. See Temp. Treas. Reg. § 1.274-5T(b)(2). Each element of a traveling expense must be substantiated through “adequate records” or by “sufficient evidence corroborating the taxpayer’s own statement.” See § 274(d)
(flush language); see also Temp. Treas. Reg. § 1.274-5T(c)(1), (2), and (3).
Petitioners provided a spreadsheet of their 2011 travel expenses. The disputed expenses involve numerous small amounts associated with toll tag charges and parking fees. These expenses do not clearly correspond with the travel destinations on petitioners’ travel logs. Moreover, when asked about several of these expenses at trial, Mr. Simpson did not provide testimony that corroborated the assertions made in petitioners’ travel logs.

Commuter fare is not deductible as a business expense, Treas. Reg. § 1.162-2, and costs related to passenger automobiles must be substantiated with carefully kept logs or records, § 274(d). Those seminars were an element in the Henrys’ recruitment of clients. Therefore, we allow Mr. Henry’s claimed deductions for the hotel expenses for years 2011 and 2012.

**Tax Year: 2026**

Yes, a taxpayer has income when a life insurance policy they thought they had transferred is terminated.

When a life insurance policy terminates, a taxpayer must recognize an indirect distribution of the insurance policy's cash surrender value as gross income under section 72, even if the taxpayer did not receive cash. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8] Gross income includes all "accessions to wealth, clearly realized, and over which the taxpayers have complete dominion." [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *7] Gross income includes nonannuity amounts received under a life insurance contract in excess of the investment in the contract. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *7]

Where a policy terminates and the life insurance company uses the policy's cash surrender value to satisfy outstanding loans against the policy, the taxpayer is treated as having received a taxable constructive distribution equal to the gain on the policy. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8] "The loan repayment is treated as if the cash value of the Policy was transferred to [the taxpayer] and he in turn repaid the outstanding loans." [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8] This prevents "policy proceeds, including previously untaxed investment returns, [from escaping] tax altogether." [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8]

However, if the taxpayer always had the ability to obtain the policy (such that the policy was always available for distribution), the termination of a plan holding the policy may not itself constitute a taxable event. [T.C. Memo. 2012-104, at *52-53]

(a) General rule. There shall be included in the gross income of an employee for the taxable year an amount equal to the cost of group-term life insurance on his life provided for part or all of such year under a policy (or policies) carried directly or indirectly by his employer (or employers); but only to the extent that such cost exceeds the sum of— (1) the cost of $50,000 of such insurance, and
(2) the amount (if any) paid by the employee toward the purchase of such insurance.
(b) Exceptions. Subsection (a) shall not apply to— (1) the cost of group-term life insurance on the life of an individual which is provided under a policy carried directly or indirectly by an employer after such individual has terminated his employment with such employer and is disabled (within the meaning of section 72(m)(7)),
(2) the cost of any portion of the group-term life insurance on the life of an employee provided during part or all of the taxable year of the employee under which— (A) the employer is directly or indirectly the beneficiary, or
(B) a person described in section 170(c) is the sole beneficiary,
for the entire period during such taxable year for which the employee receives such insurance, and
(3) the cost of any group-term life insurance which is provided under a contract to which section 72(m)(3) applies.
(c) Determination of cost of insurance. For purposes of this section and section 6052, the cost of group-term insurance on the life of an employee provided during any period shall be determined on the basis of uniform premiums (computed on the basis of 5-year age brackets) prescribed by regulations by the Secretary.

Memo. 1999-61, 77 T.C.M. (CCH) 1476. In Atwood a husband and wife held life insurance policies, and both borrowed against their respective policies; when the policies terminated, the life insurance company used their respective cash surrender values to satisfy their loans and issued both of them Forms 1099–R reflecting the gain from the surrender of their policies. This Court held that each had received a deemed distribution to the extent of the satisfied loans. Id. at 1478 (“[Any other conclusion] would permit policy proceeds, including previously untaxed investment returns, to escape tax altogether and finds no basis in the law.”); see also McGowen v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-285, aff’d, 438 F. App’x 686 (10th Cir. 2011).
Northwestern terminated the Policy on July 26, 2015, when the amount of Mr. Sawyer’s loans (both the Policy Loan and the Premium Loan) and interest eclipsed the cash surrender value of the policy. Although Mr. Sawyer did not receive any cash, the entirety of the Policy’s value having been applied against the outstanding loans, he is nonetheless treated as having received a taxable constructive distribution of $160,900.39, similarly to the taxpayers in Atwood. The loan repayment is treated as if the cash value of the Policy was transferred to Mr. Sawyer and he in turn repaid the outstanding loans.

**Tax Year: 2026**

Yes. When a life insurance policy is terminated, a taxpayer must recognize taxable income to the extent the cash surrender value of the policy exceeds the taxpayer's investment in the contract, even if the taxpayer did not receive cash. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *7-8]

Memo. 2026-33, at *7-8] Investment in the contract is defined as the amount of premiums paid less amounts received under the contract that were excludable from gross income. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *7-8]

A taxpayer must recognize an indirect distribution of an insurance policy's cash surrender value as gross income under section 72, even where the cash value was used to extinguish policy debt rather than distributed directly to the taxpayer. answers.text:
**Tax Year 2026**

# Tax Year 2026

## Factors for Determining Whether Horse Breeding Is a Business or Hobby

Under section 183, an activity is presumed to be engaged in for profit if the taxpayer has gross income exceeding deductions for 2 or more of 7 consecutive taxable years in a horse breeding activity. [26 U.S.C. § 183(d)] Otherwise, courts apply a multi-factor test examining all facts and circumstances to determine whether the taxpayer's predominant, primary or principal objective was profit. [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

The relevant factors include:

**1. Expertise and Consultation with Experts:** A taxpayer's own expertise, research, and consultation with experts may indicate a profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *17-18] The focus is whether the taxpayer received advice on "the accepted principles and economics of profitably running a business and not merely the general advice that a horse enthusiast would seek in training and showing horses as a hobby." [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *17-18]

**2. Time and Effort Devoted:** The taxpayer's substantial time and effort devoted to the activity, including physically demanding daily work rather than leisure pursuit, supports a profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

**3. Manner of Conducting the Activity:** Actions taken in a business-like manner, such as developing a business plan with calculated steps, studying the business aspects, and registering horses for sale as purebreds, support a profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27]; [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25]

**4. Personal Motives:** Having personal motives or recreational elements may indicate a hobby, but personal pleasure will not cause the activity to be classified as a hobby if other evidence shows it is engaged in for profit. [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27]

## Tax Court Application Examples

**Dennis case:** The taxpayer studied the business aspect, developed a breeding and training plan requiring 3-to-4 years, and acquired veterinary and training skills to execute his business model. Though he had personal reasons for choosing the property, he converted it into a business and sought information from others about setting up a horse breeding business. Personal friendships were instrumental to the breeding and selling activity. [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27] This supported a finding of profit objective.

**Helmick case:** The taxpayers spent 9 years suing for clear title to a purebred Arabian stallion to enable registration and sale of offspring as registered purebreds (which are more valuable). This litigation was motivated by desire to increase profits rather than personal pleasure. Each had over 8 years of breeding and boarding experience, and one served on boards of professional horse associations. They hired veterinarians to assist. [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25] Overall, these factors indicated profit objective despite some mixed considerations.

**Himmel case:** The taxpayers possessed no formal agricultural or horse breeding training, though one had decades of involvement in the Arabian horse industry with competition wins and association roles, and the other had general business experience and prior horse sales for profit. However, they failed to credibly consult with industry experts on improving profitability and lacked financial expertise in running an Arabian horse farm. While they had considerable knowledge in training, caring for, and breeding horses technically, this factor was found neutral overall. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *18]

# Tax Year 2026

## Factors for Determining Whether Horse Breeding Activity Is a Business or Hobby

**Statutory Framework**

An activity is presumed to be engaged in for profit if the gross income from the activity exceeds deductions for 2 or more of 7 consecutive taxable years ending with the taxable year in question, in the case of horse breeding and racing activities. [26 U.S.C. § 183(d)] If the activity is not engaged in for profit, deductions are limited to the extent gross income exceeds certain allowable deductions. [26 U.S.C. § 183(b)]

**Relevant Factors from Tax Court**

The Tax Court considers all facts and circumstances to determine whether the taxpayer's predominant, primary or principal objective was profit. [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22] The key factors include:

1. **Expertise and Study**: A taxpayer's own expertise, research, extensive study, and consultation with professional experts in the industry may indicate a profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *17-18]; [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25] However, merely possessing general knowledge as a horse enthusiast, without credible professional business consultation, weighs against finding a profit motive. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *18]

2. **Business Planning and Method**: Developing a business plan and taking calculated steps to execute it, including acquiring relevant skills, supports a profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27] The manner in which the activity is conducted—such as registering horses to increase their market value—also weighs in favor of a profit motive. [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25]

3. **Personal Motives**: Personal pleasure or recreational elements in conducting the activity may indicate lack of profit motive, but personal enjoyment will not prevent classification as a business if other evidence shows genuine profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27]

4. **Time and Effort**: Substantial, sustained time and effort devoted to the activity, including performing physically demanding daily work rather than leisure pursuit, supports a profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

answers.text:
# Answer for Tax Year 2026

## Factors for Determining Business versus Hobby

The relevant statute is section 183, which disallows deductions for activities not engaged in for profit except under specified limits. [26 U.S.C. § 183(a)-(d)] An activity qualifies as "engaged in for profit" if it meets the presumption under section 183(d): if gross income exceeds deductions for 3 or more of 5 consecutive taxable years (or 2 of 7 years for horse breeding/racing activities), the activity is presumed to be for profit. [26 U.S.C. § 183(d)]

When the presumption does not apply, courts examine all facts and circumstances under Treasury Regulation § 1.183-2(b), which identifies several factors:

1. **Expertise and consultation with experts**: A taxpayer's own expertise, research, study, and consultation with experts in accepted business principles and economics may indicate profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *17-18]

2. **Manner of conducting the activity**: The manner and businesslike approach to operations can indicate profit objective, including steps like registering horses to increase their market value. [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25]

3. **Time and effort devoted**: Substantial time and effort devoted to the activity, especially when physically demanding and sustained as daily work rather than leisure, supports a business finding. [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22]

4. **Personal motives**: Personal pleasure or recreational elements may weigh against finding a profit objective, though they do not necessarily defeat the business classification if other factors support it. [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27]

5. **Development of a business plan**: Studying the business aspect and developing a calculated plan for profitability supports the profit objective. [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27]

## Tax Court Application

Courts apply these factors holistically, considering all facts and circumstances. [T.C. Memo. 2026-76, at *22] A critical distinction emerges in how courts evaluate "expertise": consulting with experts means receiving advice on "accepted principles and economics of profitably running a business" rather than merely "general advice that a horse enthusiast would seek." [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *17-18] General association with knowledgeable individuals without formal professional consultation may be insufficient. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *18]

Courts have found the business factor favorable where taxpayers developed detailed business models with realistic timelines, studied the financial and operational aspects systematically, and obtained relevant experience over years—particularly when combined with actions like pursuing litigation to register horses to increase their market value. [T.C. Memo. 2009-220, at *23-25]; [T.C. Memo. 2010-216, at *26-27] Conversely, courts have weighed against the business finding where taxpayers lacked formal financial expertise, possessed only general horse industry knowledge, and failed to credibly consult with industry experts on profitability. [T.C. Memo. 2025-35, at *18]

(a) General rule. In the case of an activity engaged in by an individual or an S corporation, if such activity is not engaged in for profit, no deduction attributable to such activity shall be allowed under this chapter except as provided in this section.
(b) Deductions allowable. In the case of an activity not engaged in for profit to which subsection (a) applies, there shall be allowed— (1) the deductions which would be allowable under this chapter for the taxable year without regard to whether or not such activity is engaged in for profit, and
(2) a deduction equal to the amount of the deductions which would be allowable under this chapter for the taxable year only if such activity were engaged in for profit, but only to the extent that the gross income derived from such activity for the taxable year exceeds the deductions allowable by reason of paragraph (1).
(c) Activity not engaged in for profit defined. For purposes of this section, the term “activity not engaged in for profit” means any activity other than one with respect to which deductions are allowable for the taxable year under section 162 or under paragraph (1) or (2) of section 212.
(d) Presumption. If the gross income derived from an activity for 3 or more of the taxable years in the period of 5 consecutive taxable years which ends with the taxable year exceeds the deductions attributable to such activity (determined without regard to whether or not such activity is engaged in for profit), then, unless the Secretary establishes to the contrary, such activity shall be presumed for purposes of this chapter for such taxable year to be an activity engaged in for profit. In the case of an activity which consists in major part of the breeding, training, showing, or racing of horses, the preceding sentence shall be applied by substituting “2” for “3” and “7” for “5”.

Tax year 2026.

## Active Participation Standard

To actively participate in a rental real estate activity, you must own at least 10% of the rental property and make management decisions or arrange for others to provide services in a significant and bona fide sense. [26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(6)(A)] Management decisions that count include approving new tenants, deciding on rental terms, and approving expenditures. [IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20]

A person who fully owns and personally manages rental houses would satisfy both the ownership threshold and the management decision requirement. [26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(6)(A); IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20]

If you actively participated, you may deduct up to $25,000 of passive rental real estate loss from nonpassive income (subject to phase-out above $100,000 MAGI). [26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(1); IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20]

## Tax Court Treatment

The Tax Court has not treated full ownership and management of rental properties as automatically conferring active participation status in all cases. Instead, courts examine whether the taxpayer actually made or arranged management decisions in a significant and bona fide sense. [T.C. Memo. 2012-165, at *18-20] (holding taxpayers were "not regularly and actively involved in managing" despite ownership).

However, where taxpayers introduced credible evidence of actual involvement in management decisions—such as advertising, selecting tenants, collecting rents, and arranging repairs—courts have found active participation, even without formal real estate professional status. [IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20] (example showing active participation based on these activities); [T.C. Memo. 2024-106, at *12-13] (allowing active participation deduction where taxpayers owned and managed properties, treating them as active participants).

On brief respondent argues that petitioners did not establish that they are real estate professionals or that they actively participated in the rental activities. The fact that petitioners are not real estate
professionals has no bearing on our decision as they may deduct the claimed losses as active participants. Respondent raised the active participation requirement for the first time on brief. Accordingly, the Court understood that the real estate loss issue involved only a computation adjustment under the phaseout and the threshold rules of section 469(i). We will not allow respondent to raise the active participation requirement as a new issue posttrial because it would unduly prejudice petitioners. See Dirico v. Commissioner, 139 T.C. 396, 415–17 (2012). Accordingly, we treat petitioners as actively participating in their rental activities and hold that they may deduct $25,000 in real estate losses for 2013, 2015, and 2016, subject to the phaseout and threshold rules of section 469(i) as determined in the Rule 155 computation.

answers.question: Does a client who fully owns rental houses and manages them count as actively participating for the rental loss allowance, and how has the Tax Court treated such owners?

answers.text:
# Tax Year 2026

## Active Participation Definition

You actively participated in a rental real estate activity if you owned at least 10% of the rental property and you made management decisions or arranged for others to provide services in a significant and bona fide sense. [IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20] Management decisions that count include approving new tenants, deciding on rental terms, and approving expenditures. [IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20] Your spouse's participation counts toward your active participation. [26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(6)(D)]

A client who fully owns and manages rental houses—making tenant, rental term, and expenditure decisions—satisfies the active participation requirement.

## Tax Court Treatment

The Tax Court has consistently upheld active participation claims where taxpayers demonstrate management involvement:

- In *Willock*, the court recognized active participation based on the taxpayer's management of rental property, contrasting it with passive loss treatment of other activities. [T.C. Memo. 2010-75, at *24-25]

- In *Aboui & Mizani* (2013–2016), the court treated taxpayers as actively participating in rental activities and upheld their $25,000 deduction, stating that they "may deduct the claimed losses as active participants" without requiring real estate professional status. [T.C. Memo. 2024-106, at *12-13]

- In *Akers*, the court recognized that material participation in rental activities (when the property does not qualify as a "rental activity" under the passive activity rules) allows loss deductions. [T.C. Memo. 2010-85, at *6-7]

The Tax Court has not required full ownership or any particular ownership percentage beyond the 10% minimum stated in the statute.

answers.question: Does a client who fully owns rental houses and manages them count as actively participating for the rental loss allowance, and how has the Tax Court treated such owners?

answers.text:
# Tax Year 2026

## Active Participation Standard

To count as actively participating in rental real estate for the $25,000 loss allowance, you must own at least 10% of the rental property and make management decisions or arrange for others to provide services in a significant and bona fide sense. [26 U.S.C. § 469(i)(6)(A)] Management decisions that count include approving new tenants, deciding on rental terms, approving expenditures, and similar decisions. [IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20]

Full ownership and personal management of rental houses—such as advertising, renting the property, collecting rents, and contracting repairs—can satisfy the active participation requirement. [IRS Pub 527 (2025), p. 20]

## Tax Court Treatment

The Tax Court has treated taxpayers who fully own and manage rental properties as having actively participated. In *Mohamad Nasser Aboui & Mahyar Mizani v. Commissioner*, the Tax Court allowed deductions of $25,000 in real estate losses where petitioners were treated as actively participating in their rental activities without requiring proof they were real estate professionals. [T.C. Memo. 2024-106, at *12-13]

However, the Tax Court has also held that merely owning rental properties without substantial involvement does not establish active participation. In *Amir H. Jafarpour & Lecia R. Prang v. Commissioner*, the court found that petitioners "were not regularly and actively involved in managing" their rental properties and therefore were not entitled to loss deductions. [T.C. Memo. 2012-165, at *18-20]

The critical factor is whether you engage in regular, continuous decision-making and management activities—not ownership alone.

Yes, the farm can challenge the IRS reclassification in Tax Court. answers.text:
**Tax Year: 2026**

## Part 1: Challenging Worker Classification in Tax Court

Yes, the farm can challenge the reclassification in Tax Court. Where the Commissioner seeks to reclassify an individual as an employee for purposes of imposing employment taxes, the employer may petition Tax Court for review of the employee classification as well as the proper amount of employment tax owing as a result of classifying the worker as an employee. [T.C. Memo. 2009-234, at *5]

## Part 2: Tax Court Rulings on Farm Workers Receiving Housing and Advances

The Tax Court has held that farm workers who receive housing and wage advances are employees, not independent contractors.

In *Twin Rivers Farm, Inc. v. Commissioner*, the farm provided workers with a residence on the property, covered all job-related expenses, purchased workers' compensation and employer's liability insurance for the workers, and allowed workers to receive advances on their weekly compensation (with subsequent paychecks reduced to repay the advance). [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13] The Tax Court found these actions "far more indicative of an intention to create an employment relationship than they are of an intention to create an independent-contractor relationship." [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13] The court also noted that because the workers were long-term employees who actually resided on the farm, "it cannot be said that the relationship was transitory or temporary," which supported an employer-employee relationship. [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13]

The Tax Court concluded that the workers were employees for purposes of Federal employment taxes. [T.C. Memo. 2012-184, at *11-13]

issue. Furthermore, the workers actually maintained their primary residence on
petitioner's property in a trailer provided to them by petitioner. Although there is

creating an explicit permanent employment relationship, the relationship in

transitory or temporary. Therefore, we find that this factor is also supportive of an
employer-employee relationship.
7. Relationship the Parties Thought They Created
Petitioner contends that the relationship created by the parties was intended
to be that of a business and independent contractors. However, the relationship
between petitioner and the workers does not support such a characterization. The
record indicates that petitioner purchased workers' compensation and employer's
liability insurance for the years at issue.
In addition, petitioner covered all of the
job-related expenses necessary for the workers to perform their duties. Petitioner
even provided a residence on the property for the workers and allowed the workers
to receive advances on their compensation. These actions are far more indicative
of an intention to create an employment relationship than they are of an intention
to create an independent-contractor relationship. Therefore, this factor also
supports the existence of an employer-employee relationship.

of the facts and circumstances particular to this case, we hold that the workers

**Tax Year 2026**

## Part 1: Recordkeeping Requirements for Travel Expenses

A taxpayer must keep records sufficient to identify "the amount and nature of any expenditure" and preserve supporting documents, especially for large or exceptional expenditures. [26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2)] Detailed records of small expenditures such as tips will not be required. [26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2)]

Travel expenses are subject to heightened substantiation requirements. A deduction for traveling expenses is permitted only to the extent the taxpayer proves: (1) the amount of each expenditure for traveling away from home, (2) the date of departure and return for each trip and the number of days spent on business, (3) the destination or locality of travel, and (4) the business reason for travel or the expected business benefit. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *18-19] Each element must be substantiated through "adequate records" or by "sufficient evidence corroborating the taxpayer's own statement." [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *18-19]

## Part 2: Acceptance of Taxpayer-Prepared Spreadsheets for Tolls and Parking Charges

The Tax Court has **rejected** a taxpayer-prepared spreadsheet of toll and parking charges where the expenses did not clearly correspond with travel destinations on the travel logs and the taxpayer's testimony did not corroborate the assertions in the logs. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19] The Court found the spreadsheet lacked the specificity and detail required under the regulations. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19] Accordingly, the taxpayers could deduct only the amounts the IRS allowed.

A spreadsheet alone is insufficient; tolls and parking charges must be supported by adequate records or corroborating evidence tied to documented travel destinations and business purposes.

**Tax year 2026**

## Substantiation Requirements for Travel Expenses

Travel expenses are subject to heightened substantiation requirements. [26 U.S.C. § 274(d)] A taxpayer must prove: (1) the amount of each expenditure for traveling away from home; (2) the date of departure and return for each trip and the number of days spent on business; (3) the destination or locality of travel; and (4) the business reason for travel or the expected business benefit to be derived. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *18]

The burden of proof is on the taxpayer to show that expenses were not only paid or incurred but also that they constitute ordinary and necessary business expenses. [26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2)] One method for substantiating expenses is through preparation of a daily diary or record of expenditures maintained in sufficient detail to enable ready identification of the amount and nature of any expenditure, and preservation of supporting documents, especially for large or exceptional expenditures. [26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2)] Detailed records of small expenditures such as tips will not be required. [26 CFR 1.162-17(d)(2)]

IRS Publication 463 recommends attaching receipted bills for all lodging and any other expenses of $75.00 or more. [IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 40]

## Tax Court Treatment of Spreadsheets for Tolls and Parking

The Tax Court has **rejected** a taxpayer-prepared spreadsheet of toll and parking charges as insufficient substantiation. In *Kyle D. Simpson & Christen Simpson v. Commissioner*, the court held that petitioners failed to satisfy their burden of substantiating travel expenses where a spreadsheet of toll tag charges and parking fees did not clearly correspond with travel destinations on their travel logs, and the taxpayer's trial testimony did not corroborate the assertions in the logs. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19] The court found the spreadsheet lacked the specificity and detail required by regulation. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *19]

**Tax year: 2026**

## Constructive Receipt Doctrine

Income is constructively received in the taxable year during which it is credited to the taxpayer's account, set apart for the taxpayer, or otherwise made available so that the taxpayer may draw upon it at any time, or so that the taxpayer could have drawn upon it during the taxable year if notice of intention to withdraw had been given. [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)] However, income is not constructively received if the taxpayer's control of its receipt is subject to substantial limitations or restrictions. [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)]

Examples of constructive receipt include: matured and payable interest coupons [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)]; dividends made unqualifiedly subject to the demand of a shareholder [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)]; dividends or interest credited on savings bank deposits [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)]; and accrued interest on unwithdrawn insurance policy dividends in the first taxable year during which such interest may be withdrawn. [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)]

The doctrine addresses when, not whether, income is realized by a cash basis taxpayer. [T.C. Memo. 2007-271, at *7-9]

## Application to Terminated Life Insurance Policy

Yes, the Tax Court has applied constructive receipt to a terminated life insurance policy. In *Jonathan D. Sawyer v. Commissioner*, the Court held that when a life insurance policy terminated and the insurance company used the policy's cash surrender value to satisfy outstanding policy loans, the taxpayer constructively received a taxable distribution to the extent of the satisfied loans, even though the taxpayer received no cash. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8] The Court treated the loan repayment as if the cash value of the policy was transferred to the taxpayer and the taxpayer in turn repaid the outstanding loans. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8]

Amounts payable with respect to interest coupons which have matured and are payable but which have not been cashed are constructively received in the taxable year during which the coupons mature, unless it can be shown that there are no funds available for payment of the interest during such year. Dividends on corporate stock are constructively received when unqualifiedly made subject to the demand of the shareholder. However, if a dividend is declared payable on December 31 and the corporation followed its usual practice of paying the dividends by checks mailed so that the shareholders would not receive them until January of the following year, such dividends are not considered to have been constructively received in December. Generally, the amount of dividends or interest credited on savings bank deposits or to shareholders of organizations such as building and loan associations or cooperative banks is income to the depositors or shareholders for the taxable year when credited. However, if any portion of such dividends or interest is not subject to withdrawal at the time credited, such portion is not constructively received and does not constitute income to the depositor or shareholder until the taxable year in which the portion first may be withdrawn. Accordingly, if, under a bonus or forfeiture plan, a portion of the dividends or interest is accumulated and may not be withdrawn until the maturity of the plan, the crediting of such portion to the account of the shareholder or depositor does not constitute constructive receipt. In this case, such credited portion is income to the depositor or shareholder in the year in which the plan matures. However, in the case of certain deposits made after December 31, 1970, in banks, domestic building and loan associations, and similar financial institutions, the ratable inclusion rules of section 1232(a)(3) apply. See § 1.1232-3A. Accrued interest on unwithdrawn insurance policy dividends is gross income to the taxpayer for the first taxable year during which such interest may be withdrawn by him.

answers.text:
**2026 Tax Year**

**Constructive Receipt of Income**

Income is constructively received by a taxpayer in the taxable year during which it is credited to his account, set apart for him, or otherwise made available so that he may draw upon it at any time, or so that he could have drawn upon it during the taxable year if notice of intention to withdraw had been given. [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)] However, income is not constructively received if the taxpayer's control of its receipt is subject to substantial limitations or restrictions. [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)]

Examples of constructive receipt include: amounts payable with respect to interest coupons that have matured and are payable but have not been cashed (unless no funds are available for payment); dividends on corporate stock when unqualifiedly made subject to the demand of the shareholder; and the amount of dividends or interest credited on savings bank deposits or similar institutions when credited, unless the portion is not subject to withdrawal at the time credited. [26 CFR 1.451-2(b)]

Additionally, for annuities and life insurance contracts, rules similar to those governing constructive receipt apply. [26 U.S.C. § 72(o)(3)]

**Tax Court Application to Terminated Life Insurance Policies**

Yes, the Tax Court has applied the constructive receipt doctrine to a terminated life insurance policy. In *Jonathan D. Sawyer v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo. 2026-33, the Court held that when a life insurance policy terminated and the insurance company used the policy's cash surrender value to satisfy outstanding policy loans, the taxpayer constructively received a taxable distribution to the extent of the satisfied loans, even though he received no cash. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8] The Court reasoned that "the loan repayment is treated as if the cash value of the Policy was transferred to Mr. Sawyer and he in turn repaid the outstanding loans," citing its earlier decision in *Atwood v. Commissioner*. [T.C. Memo. 2026-33, at *8]

**Tax year 2026**

## Code Rule on Personal Expenses

Section 262 of the Internal Revenue Code provides the governing rule, but it is not quoted in the sources provided. However, the sources establish that personal expenses are generally not deductible.

## Tax Court Ruling on Streaming Subscriptions

The Tax Court has directly ruled on this issue. In *Suleiman Sami v. Commissioner*, the taxpayer claimed deductions for television and video streaming expenses (DirectTV, TimeWarner/Spectrum, WWE, Apple, Netflix, and Hulu) totaling $2,896, $3,211, and $3,766 for tax years 2019, 2020, and 2021, respectively, arguing they were "market research" for his influencer and ticket-selling businesses. [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15]

The Tax Court held that **these expenses are not deductible**. The court found that "viewing television and online videos is a common source of personal enjoyment" and that the taxpayer's testimony did not convince the court "that these payments were directly related to his business." [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15] The court cited the principle that "payments for television and cable bills are not deductible business expenses if they were not directly related to a taxpayer's business." [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15]

The broader principle: expenses under section 162(a) are deductible only if "primarily undertaken for business, instead of personal, purposes." [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *16-17]

**Tax Year 2026**

**Personal Expenses Under the Code**

The Internal Revenue Code does not directly define or broadly prohibit deduction of personal expenses. However, 26 U.S.C. § 263A(h)(2) addresses one category: it allows writers, photographers, and artists to deduct "qualified creative expenses" (those that would otherwise be deductible) but excludes expenses related to printing, photographic plates, motion picture films, video tapes, or similar items. [26 U.S.C. § 263A(h)(2)]

Additionally, 26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(6) denies deductions for out-of-pocket expenditures made to influence legislation. [26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(6)]

Commissioner*, an influencer claimed deductions for television and video streaming expenses (DirectTV, TimeWarner/Spectrum, WWE, Apple, Netflix, and Hulu totaling $2,896–$3,766 annually) labeled as "market research" for learning about entertainment events and social media trends. The Court held: "Viewing television and online videos is a common source of personal enjoyment, and we are not convinced from Mr. Sami's testimony that these payments were directly related to his business" and concluded "these are personal expenses that Mr. Sami is not entitled to deduct." [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15] The Court cited the principle that "Payments for television and cable bills are not deductible business expenses if they were not directly related to a taxpayer's business." [T.C. Memo. 2026-69, at *15]

We likewise note that we “bear[] heavily . . . upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making” by failing to maintain contemporaneous business records. Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d at 544. Because it was reasonable from
a business perspective to have at least one of the four phones, we will allow Mr. Sami to deduct 25% of his reported expenses for cell phone service.
However, we have no basis for determining that the purported charges for cell phone equipment were for business rather than personal use and will not allow deductions for those reported expenses.
C.
Television and Video Streaming
Mr. Sami claimed deductions of $2,896, $3,211, and $3,766 for television and video streaming expenses for tax years 2019, 2020, and 2021, respectively, under the label of “market research.” He argues that the expenses were for business purposes because they allowed him to learn about entertainment events, to which he could then sell tickets, and trends that might help him in his social media influencer activities.

contexts.text:
marketing ones, and it is likely that he derived considerable personal status from these brushings with the famous. While it is true that some of the interactions (as Mr. Sami points out) were embarrassing––the dropped pass from Brady, the flubbed return from McEnroe––they still created stories and personal prestige and were likely motivated by charitable intent as originally reported. Yes, Mr. Sami was a Jets supporter, and so no fan of Brady, but we were still left with the impression that he enjoyed interacting with him. Overall, our impression after Mr. Sami’s testimony was that his motives for buying these experiences were primarily personal, rather than hard-headed business ones. Consequently, he cannot deduct their costs under section 162(a).
Mr. Sami points out that these celebrity interactions had positive consequences for his business. For example, the pictures he took with celebrities increased his views and followers, which eventually purportedly increased his advertising revenue. But this is not dispositive, because the question is not whether the expenses had any effect on his revenues. If that were the standard, it would be met by countless clearly personal expenses, such as a comedian getting good material for her standup act while on a European vacation. Instead, the question is whether these expenses meet the necessary condition of being primarily undertaken for business, instead of personal reasons. We hold that they do not.
Mr. Sami also argues that these expenses are usual, and so ordinary, expenses for influencers. Disney-focused influencers, for example, pay to go to film premieres, Mr. Sami says, so they can then post videos and images of the premieres and generate income. This may be, but even if Mr. Sami’s expenses are typical influencer expenses, they are still not deductible under section 162(a), since they were not incurred primarily for business purposes.

contexts.text:
We come now to the main event.
Expenses are deductible under section 162(a) only if they are primarily undertaken for business, instead of personal, purposes. Walliser v. Commissioner, 72 T.C. 433, 437–38 (1979). In the textbookfavorite Danville Plywood, for example, employees of a plywood manufacturing company went on a weekend trip to the Super Bowl with some customers, and the company reported the employees’ expenses as business expenses. Danville Plywood Corp. v. United States, 899 F.2d 3, 5–6 (Fed. Cir. 1990). The court held that the employees’ expenses were not deductible under section 162(a), since the trip was “a group social excursion with business playing a subsidiary role.” Danville Plywood, 899 F.2d at 9. By contrast, in Tucker, a struggling fashion label entrepreneur appeared on a local public television show with models wearing the label’s clothes. Tucker v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo.
2023-87, at *4–5, aff’d, No. 24-1147, 2025 WL 511651 (1st Cir. Jan. 6, 2025). We held that, under section 162(a), the entrepreneur could deduct the expenses for this appearance, since the entrepreneur’s “primary motive or purpose in appearing on the show was to increase [the label’s] visibility and in turn generate sales of [its] products.” Tucker, T.C. Memo. 2023-87, at *14.
