answers.text:
Tax year: 2026

Your client can exclude $250,000 of the gain from the sale of her principal residence.

To qualify for the exclusion under § 121(a), a taxpayer must have owned and used the property as her principal residence for periods aggregating 2 years or more during the 5-year period ending on the date of sale. [26 U.S.C. § 121(a)] Your client meets this requirement, having owned and lived in the house for 3 of the last 5 years.

For an unmarried taxpayer who meets the ownership and use tests, the maximum exclusion is $250,000. [26 U.S.C. § 121(a)] Since your client's realized gain of $200,000 does not exceed this maximum, she may exclude the entire $200,000.

# Tax Year 2026

## Part 1: Maximum Deduction for Student Loan Interest

The maximum deduction for student loan interest is $2,500 per taxable year. [26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(1)]

## Part 2: Income Phase-Out Limits for Student Loan Interest Deduction

Yes, the client's income affects the deduction. The deduction is reduced based on modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). [26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2)(A)]

For a single filer, the deduction begins to phase out when MAGI exceeds $50,000, and is completely eliminated at $65,000 MAGI ($50,000 + $15,000). [26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2)(B)]

For joint filers, the phase-out begins at $100,000 MAGI and is completely eliminated at $130,000 MAGI ($100,000 + $30,000). [26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2)(B)]

Modified adjusted gross income is calculated without regard to the section 221 deduction itself and without regard to sections 85(c), 911, 931, and 933, but after application of sections 86, 135, 137, 219, and 469. [26 U.S.C. § 221(b)(2)(C)]

Additionally, no deduction is allowed if another taxpayer can claim a dependency deduction for the client for the calendar year in which the client's taxable year begins. [26 U.S.C. § 221(c)]

**2026**

**Part 1: Deduction of Business Investigation Expenses Under IRC Section 195**

Your client's $8,000 investigation expense is a "start-up expenditure" because it was paid in connection with investigating the creation of an active trade or business, and would be deductible if paid in connection with an existing business. [26 U.S.C. § 195(c)(1)]

Your client cannot deduct the full $8,000 in the first year. Instead, if your client makes an election under section 195(b), the deduction is limited to the lesser of (i) $8,000 or (ii) $5,000 reduced by the amount by which start-up expenditures exceed $50,000. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(A)] Since the $8,000 does not exceed $50,000, the reduction is zero, so your client may deduct $5,000 in the year the business begins. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(A)(ii)]

The remaining $3,000 must be deducted ratably over 180 months beginning with the month the business begins. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(B)]

The election must be made by the tax filing deadline (including extensions) for the year the business begins. [26 U.S.C. § 195(d)(1)]

In December 2003, H exchanges, in a like-kind exchange, Automobile X plus $15,000 cash for new Automobile Y that will also be used solely in H's business. Automobile Y is 50-percent bonus depreciation property for purposes of section 168(k)(4). Both automobiles are depreciated using the double declining balance method, the half-year convention, and a 5-year recovery period. Pursuant to § 1.168(k)-1(g)(3)(ii) and paragraph (k)(2)(i) of this section, H decided to apply § 1.168(i)-6 to the exchange of Automobile X for Automobile Y, the replacement MACRS property. The relinquished automobile section 280F limit for 2003 for Automobile X is $1,775. The replacement automobile section 280F limit for Automobile Y is $10,710. The exchanged basis for Automobile Y is $17,315 ($30,000 less total depreciation allowable of $12,685 (($3,060 for 2000, $4,900 for 2001, $2,950 for 2002, and $1,775 for 2003)). Without taking section 280F into account, the additional first year depreciation deduction for the remaining exchanged basis is $8,658 ($17,315 × 0.5). Because this amount is less than $8,935 ($10,710 (the replacement automobile section 280F limit for 2003 for Automobile Y) − $1,775 (the depreciation allowable for Automobile X for 2003)), the additional first year depreciation deduction for the exchanged basis is $8,658. No depreciation deduction is allowable in 2003 for the depreciable exchanged basis because the depreciation deductions taken for Automobile X and the remaining exchanged basis exceed the exchanged automobile section 280F limit. An additional first year depreciation deduction of $277 is allowable for the excess basis of $15,000 in Automobile Y. Thus, at the end of 2003 the adjusted depreciable basis in Automobile Y is $23,379 comprised of adjusted depreciable exchanged basis of $8,657 ($17,315 (exchanged basis) − $8,658 (additional first year depreciation for exchanged basis)) and of an adjusted depreciable excess basis of $14,723 ($15,000 (excess basis) − $277 (additional first year depreciation for 2003)).

answers.question: My client spent $8,000 investigating a business before it opened. Can they deduct that in the first year?

answers.text:
**Tax year: 2026**

Your client cannot deduct the full $8,000 in the first year. Instead, the amount is subject to the start-up expenditure rules.

The $8,000 qualifies as a start-up expenditure because it was "paid or incurred in connection with investigating the creation or acquisition of an active trade or business." [26 U.S.C. § 195(c)(1)]

If your client elects to deduct start-up expenditures, they may deduct in the year the business begins the lesser of: (1) the start-up expenditures, or (2) $5,000 reduced by the amount the expenditures exceed $50,000. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(A)]

Since the $8,000 does not exceed $50,000, the reduction does not apply, and your client can deduct $5,000 in the first year. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(A)]

The remaining $3,000 must be deducted ratably over a 180-month period beginning with the month the active trade or business begins. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(B)]

The election must be made no later than the time prescribed for filing the return for the year the business begins, including extensions. [26 U.S.C. § 195(d)(1)]

Expenses paid in investigating the creation of an active trade or business are "start-up expenditures" under Section 195(c)(1)(A)(i). [26 U.S.C. § 195(c)(1)]

If your client elects to deduct start-up expenditures under Section 195(b), they may deduct in the year the business begins the lesser of: (i) the start-up expenditures, or (ii) $5,000 reduced (but not below zero) by the amount by which start-up expenditures exceed $50,000. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(A)] 

Since your client's start-up expenditures of $8,000 do not exceed $50,000, the deductible amount in the first year is the full $5,000. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(A)]

The remainder of $3,000 ($8,000 − $5,000) must be amortized ratably over the 180-month period beginning with the month the active trade or business begins. [26 U.S.C. § 195(b)(1)(B)]

The election must be made by the time prescribed for filing the return for the taxable year in which the business begins, including extensions. [26 U.S.C. § 195(d)(1)]

answers.question: My client is 45 and took $20,000 out of a 401(k). What extra tax applies?

answers.text:
**Tax year 2026**

An additional tax of 10 percent applies to your client's early distribution from the 401(k).

The additional tax is calculated as 10 percent of the portion of the distribution includible in gross income. [26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(1)] On a $20,000 distribution, this means an additional $2,000 in tax, assuming the entire amount is includible in gross income.

Your client does not qualify for any of the statutory exceptions to this 10 percent penalty, as those require the taxpayer to be age 59½ or older, disabled, or receiving substantially equal periodic payments. [26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(2)] Since your client is 45, none of these exceptions apply.

answers.text:
**2026 Tax Year**

Your client is subject to a 10 percent additional tax on the early distribution. [26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(1)]

The additional tax applies to the full $20,000 because:

1. Your client is under age 59½, so the age exception does not apply. [26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(2)] (the exception for distributions after age 59½ is implied in the statute's structure for early distribution penalties)

2. The $20,000 is from a qualified retirement plan (401(k)), triggering the 10 percent additional tax on the portion includible in gross income. [26 U.S.C. § 72(t)(1)]

The additional tax is **$2,000** (10% × $20,000), assuming the full amount is includible in gross income and no other exceptions apply.

answers.text:
**Tax Year: 2026**

An employer-provided educational assistance program allows an employee to exclude up to $5,250 of educational assistance per calendar year from gross income. [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(2)]

Since the employer paid $7,000 of tuition, the employee may exclude $5,250 and must include the remaining $1,750 in gross income.

This assumes the payment qualifies under a valid educational assistance program meeting the requirements of section 127(b) (separate written plan, non-discriminatory eligibility, restrictions on shareholder/owner benefits, no choice between education and other remuneration, and notice to employees). [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(1), (b)]

**Answer: $1,750 is taxable to the employee.**

answers.question: An employer paid $7,000 of an employee's tuition under an educational assistance program. How much is taxable to the employee?

answers.text:
Tax year: 2026

Under section 127, an employer-provided educational assistance program allows an employee to exclude amounts paid by the employer for educational assistance. [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(1)] However, the exclusion is limited to $5,250 per calendar year. [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(2)]

Since the employer paid $7,000 in tuition and the maximum exclusion is $5,250, the employee may exclude only $5,250 from gross income. [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(2)] The remaining $1,750 ($7,000 - $5,250) is taxable to the employee.

answers.question: An employer paid $7,000 of an employee's tuition under an educational assistance program. How much is taxable to the employee?

answers.text:
**Tax Year 2026**

Under IRC § 127(a)(1), an employee may exclude from gross income amounts paid by the employer for educational assistance furnished pursuant to a qualifying program. [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(1)] However, IRC § 127(a)(2) imposes a $5,250 maximum annual exclusion per employee. [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(2)]

Since the employer paid $7,000 in tuition and the maximum exclusion is $5,250, the employee may exclude only $5,250 from gross income. [26 U.S.C. § 127(a)(2)] The remaining $1,750 ($7,000 − $5,250) is taxable to the employee.

**Answer: $1,750 is taxable to the employee** (assuming the educational assistance program meets the requirements of IRC § 127(b)).

**Part 1: Contemporaneous Written Acknowledgment Requirement for Charitable Contributions of $250 or More**

No deduction is allowed for any charitable contribution of $250 or more unless the taxpayer substantiates the contribution by a contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the donee organization. [26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(A)]

The acknowledgment must include: (i) the amount of cash and a description (but not value) of any property other than cash contributed; (ii) whether the donee organization provided any goods or services in consideration for the contribution; and (iii) a description and good faith estimate of the value of any goods or services provided, or if the goods or services consist solely of intangible religious benefits, a statement to that effect. [26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(B)]

An acknowledgment is contemporaneous if the taxpayer obtains it on or before the earlier of: (i) the date the taxpayer files a return for the taxable year in which the contribution was made, or (ii) the due date (including extensions) for filing such return. [26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(C)]

**Tax year: 2026**

**Part 1: How an Employer Values Personal Use Under the Cents-Per-Mile Rule**

The value of an employee's personal use of a company car under the cents-per-mile rule is calculated by multiplying the standard mileage rate (from the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure) by the total number of miles the vehicle is driven by the employee for personal purposes. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)] The standard mileage rate must be applied prospectively from the first day of the taxable year following publication of the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)] 

When a tiered mileage rate applies (different rates for different mileage brackets), the rate is applied separately to personal miles within each bracket, independent of business miles. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)] For example, if the rate is 24 cents per mile for the first 15,000 miles and 11 cents per mile for all miles over 15,000, and an employee drives 20,000 personal miles, the value is ($0.24 × 15,000) + ($0.11 × 5,000) = $4,150. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)]

**Part 2: What the Cents-Per-Mile Rate Covers**

The cents-per-mile rate includes the fair market value of maintenance of, and insurance for, the vehicle. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(i)] 

For miles driven in the United States, Canada, or Mexico, the cents-per-mile rate includes the fair market value of fuel provided by the employer. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(ii)(A)] If the employer does not provide fuel, the rate may be reduced by no more than 5.5 cents or the amount specified in an applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(ii)(A)]

For miles driven outside the United States, Canada, or Mexico, the fair market value of fuel provided by the employer is not included in the cents-per-mile rate, so the rate may be reduced by no more than 5.5 cents or the amount specified in an applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(ii)(B)]

Any service not specifically identified in the regulation (such as chauffeur services) is not reflected in the cents-per-mile rate and must be valued separately. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(iii)]

## Part 1: How an Employer Values Personal Use Under the Cents-Per-Mile Rule

An employer values an employee's personal use of a company car by multiplying the standard mileage rate (cents-per-mile rate) by the total number of miles the vehicle is driven by the employee for personal purposes. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)]

The cents-per-mile rate is applied prospectively from the first day of the taxable year following publication of the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)]

The standard mileage rate must be applied to personal miles independent of business miles. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)] For example, if the standard mileage rate is 24 cents per mile for the first 15,000 miles and 11 cents per mile for miles over 15,000, and an employee drives 20,000 personal miles and 45,000 business miles, the value of personal use is $4,150 ((15,000 × $0.24) + (5,000 × $0.11)). [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)]

The employer must include in the employee's income an amount equal to the product of the number of personal miles driven and the appropriate cents-per-mile rate. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(4)] Unless additional services are provided, the employer may not include a greater amount—for example, the employer may not include 100 percent of all business and personal miles. answers.text:
**Tax year: 2026**

## Part 1: How an employer values personal use under the cents-per-mile rule

Under the cents-per-mile valuation rule, an employer values an employee's personal use of a company car by multiplying the standard mileage rate (published in the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure) by the total number of miles the employee drives for personal purposes. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)] The standard mileage rate must be applied to personal miles independently of business miles. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)]

The rule applies if the employer provides a vehicle that either: (A) the employer reasonably expects will be regularly used in the employer's trade or business throughout the calendar year, or (B) is actually driven at least 10,000 miles in the year and is primarily used by employees. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)]

The cents-per-mile rate may not be used if the vehicle's fair market value exceeds $50,000, as adjusted by section 280F(d)(7). [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(1)(iii)(A)]

## Part 2: What the cents-per-mile rate covers

The cents-per-mile rate includes the fair market value of maintenance and insurance for the vehicle. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(i)]

For miles driven in the United States, Canada, or Mexico, the cents-per-mile rate includes the fair market value of fuel provided by the employer. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(ii)(A)] If the employer does not provide fuel, the cents-per-mile rate may be reduced by no more than 5.5 cents per mile or the amount specified in an applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(ii)(A)]

The fair market value of any other service provided by the employer with respect to the vehicle is not reflected in the cents-per-mile rate. [26 CFR 1.61-21(e)(3)(iii)]

Tax year: 2026

To be an accountable plan, an employer's reimbursement or allowance arrangement must meet three requirements:

1. **Business connection**: Your expenses must have a business connection—that is, you must have paid or incurred deductible expenses while performing services as an employee of your employer. [IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 42]

2. **Adequate accounting**: You must adequately account to your employer for these expenses within a reasonable period of time. [IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 42] You adequately account by giving your employer a statement of expense, an account book, a diary, or a similar record in which you entered each expense at or near the time you had it, along with documentary evidence (such as receipts) of your travel, mileage, and other employee business expenses. [IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 43]

3. **Return of excess**: You must return any excess reimbursement or allowance within a reasonable period of time. [IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 42]

Under the regulation, an arrangement must also meet requirements regarding business connection, substantiation, and returning amounts in excess of expenses. [26 CFR 1.62-2(c)(1)]

answers.question: What makes an expense reimbursement arrangement an accountable plan?

answers.text:
**Tax Year 2026**

An expense reimbursement arrangement qualifies as an accountable plan if it meets three requirements:

**1. Business Connection:** The arrangement must provide advances, allowances, or reimbursements only for business expenses that are allowable as deductions under part VI (section 161 and following), subchapter B, chapter 1 of the Code, and that are paid or incurred by the employee. [26 CFR 1.62-2(d)(1)]

**2. Substantiation:** The arrangement must require the employee to substantiate the expenses covered by the arrangement to the payor. [26 CFR 1.62-2(e)(1)]

**3. Return of Excess Amounts:** The arrangement must require the employee to return to the payor within a reasonable period of time any amount paid under the arrangement in excess of the expenses substantiated. [26 CFR 1.62-2(f)(1)]

These three requirements must all be satisfied. [26 CFR 1.62-2(c)(1)]

**Note on written plans:** An accountable plan does not necessarily have to be in writing, but there must be some extrinsic evidence indicating that such a plan exists—for example, a formal process of collecting documentation and reimbursing exact amounts. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *16]

**Tax year 2026**

An expense reimbursement arrangement qualifies as an accountable plan if it meets three requirements:

**1. Business Connection:** The arrangement must provide advances, allowances, or reimbursements only for business expenses that are allowable as deductions under part VI (section 161 and following) of the Internal Revenue Code, and that are paid or incurred by the employee in connection with the performance of services as an employee. **3. Return of Excess Amounts:** The arrangement must require the employee to return to the payor within a reasonable period of time any amount paid under the arrangement in excess of the expenses substantiated. [26 CFR 1.62-2(f)(1)]

An arrangement that fails to require substantiation or that provides the employee the right to retain any amount in excess of substantiated expenses will not be treated as a reimbursement or other expense allowance arrangement. [26 CFR 1.62-2(b)]

While an accountable plan does not necessarily have to be in writing, there must be at least some extrinsic evidence indicating that such a plan exists, such as a formal process of collecting documentation to substantiate expenses and reimbursing the exact amounts associated with those expenses. [T.C. Memo. 2023-4, at *16]

(7) Limitation on deductions where combination of defined contribution plan and defined benefit plan. (A) In general. If amounts are deductible under the foregoing paragraphs of this subsection (other than paragraph (5)) in connection with 1 or more defined contribution plans and 1 or more defined benefit plans or in connection with trusts or plans described in 2 or more of such paragraphs, the total amount deductible in a taxable year under such plans shall not exceed the greater of— (i) 25 percent of the compensation otherwise paid or accrued during the taxable year to the beneficiaries under such plans, or
(ii) the amount of contributions made to or under the defined benefit plans to the extent such contributions do not exceed the amount of employer contributions necessary to satisfy the minimum funding standard provided by section 412 with respect to any such defined benefit plans for the plan year which ends with or within such taxable year (or for any prior plan year).
A defined contribution plan which is a pension plan shall not be treated as failing to provide definitely determinable benefits merely by limiting employer contributions to amounts deductible under this section. In the case of a defined benefit plan which is a single employer plan, the amount necessary to satisfy the minimum funding standard provided by section 412 shall not be less than the excess (if any) of the plan’s funding target (as defined in section 430(d)(1)) over the value of the plan’s assets (as determined under section 430(g)(3)).
(B) Carryover of contributions in excess of the deductible limit. Any amount paid under the plans in any taxable year in excess of the limitation of subparagraph (A) shall be deductible in the succeeding taxable years in order of time, but the amount so deductible under this subparagraph in any 1 such succeeding taxable year together with the amount allowable under subparagraph (A) shall not exceed 25 percent of the compensation otherwise paid or accrued during such taxable year to the beneficiaries under the plans.

(4) Allocations. (A) In general. Not later than January 1, 2025, the Secretary shall establish a program to allocate amounts of environmental justice capacity limitation to applicable facilities. In establishing such program and to carry out the purposes of this subsection, the Secretary shall provide procedures to allow for an efficient allocation process, including, when determined appropriate, consideration of multiple projects in a single application if such projects will be placed in service by a single taxpayer.
(B) Limitation. The amount of environmental justice capacity limitation allocated by the Secretary under subparagraph (A) during any calendar year shall not exceed the annual capacity limitation with respect to such year.
(C) Annual capacity limitation. For purposes of this paragraph, the term “annual capacity limitation” means 1.8 gigawatts of direct current capacity for each calendar year during the period beginning on January 1, 2025, and ending on December 31 of the applicable year (as defined in section 45Y(d)(3)), and zero thereafter.
(D) Carryover of unused limitation. (i) In general. If the annual capacity limitation for any calendar year exceeds the aggregate amount allocated for such year under this paragraph, such limitation for the succeeding calendar year shall be increased by the amount of such excess. No amount may be carried under the preceding sentence to any calendar year after the third calendar year following the applicable year (as defined in section 45Y(d)(3)).
(ii) Carryover from section 48 for calendar year 2025. If the annual capacity limitation for calendar year 2024 under section 48(e)(4)(D) exceeds the aggregate amount allocated for such year under such section, such excess amount may be carried over and applied to the annual capacity limitation under this subsection for calendar year 2025. The annual capacity limitation for calendar year 2025 shall be increased by the amount of such excess.

For a 401(k) plan, the required beginning date is April 1 following the calendar year in which the participant attains age 73. [26 CFR 1.401(a)(9)-2(a)(3)]

Since your client turns 74 in 2026, she attained age 73 in 2025. Therefore, her required beginning date is April 1, 2026. [26 CFR 1.401(a)(9)-2(a)(3)]

She must begin taking required minimum distributions by that date.

Thus, even if payments have been made before the employee's required beginning date, the rules of § 1.401(a)(9)-3 will apply if the employee dies before that date. For example, if A is an employee who retires in 2023, the calendar year A attains age 71, and begins receiving installment distributions from a profit-sharing plan over a period not exceeding the joint life and last survivor expectancy of A and A's spouse, benefits are not treated as having begun in accordance with section 401(a)(9)(A)(ii) until April 1, 2026 (the April 1 following the calendar year in which A attains age 73). Consequently, if A dies before April 1, 2026 (A's required beginning date), distributions after A's death must be made in accordance with § 1.401(a)(9)-3 (addressing payments to beneficiaries pursuant to section 401(a)(9)(B)(ii), (iii), or (iv), whichever applies, in cases in which required distributions have not begun) rather than section 401(a)(9)(B)(i) (addressing payments to beneficiaries in cases in which required distributions have begun). Yes, your clients could deduct all of the mortgage interest on their 2016 joint return.

answers.question: My married clients bought their home in 2012 with a $900,000 mortgage. On their 2016 joint return, could they deduct all of the mortgage interest?

answers.text:
**Tax year: 2016**

Yes, your clients could deduct all of their mortgage interest on their 2016 joint return.

The $900,000 mortgage is acquisition indebtedness (incurred in acquiring the home in 2012 and secured by it). [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(3)(B)(i)] The limitation on acquisition indebtedness is $1,000,000 for married individuals filing a joint return. [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(3)(B)(ii)] Since their $900,000 mortgage does not exceed $1,000,000, the interest paid on the full amount qualifies as deductible qualified residence interest. [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(3)(A)]

**Tax year 2016**

For your married clients filing jointly in 2016, they could deduct all of their mortgage interest subject to the acquisition indebtedness limitation.

Their $900,000 mortgage qualifies as acquisition indebtedness because it was incurred in acquiring a qualified residence and is secured by that residence. [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(3)(B)(i)]

For married individuals filing a joint return, the aggregate amount treated as acquisition indebtedness cannot exceed $1,000,000. [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(3)(B)(ii)] Since their mortgage balance of $900,000 is below this $1,000,000 limit, the full amount of interest paid on this indebtedness qualifies as deductible qualified residence interest. [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(3)(A)]

Yes, they could deduct all of the mortgage interest on their 2016 joint return.

**Part 1: Clean Vehicle Credit Eligibility for Two Personal-Use Electric Vehicles**

To claim the clean vehicle credit, each vehicle must meet the definition of a "new clean vehicle." [26 U.S.C. § 30D(a)] The statutory requirements include:

- Original use commences with the taxpayer [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(A)]
- Acquired for use or lease by the taxpayer and not for resale [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(B)]
- Made by a qualified manufacturer [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(C)]
- Treated as a motor vehicle under title II of the Clean Air Act [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(D)]
- Gross vehicle weight rating less than 14,000 pounds [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(E)]
- Propelled to a significant extent by an electric motor drawing electricity from a battery with at least 7 kilowatt-hour capacity, capable of external recharge [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(F)]
- Final assembly within North America [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(G)]
- Seller furnishes required reporting information [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(H)]

Additionally, for vehicles placed in service after December 31, 2023, the vehicle cannot include battery components manufactured or assembled by a foreign entity of concern. [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(7)(B)] For vehicles placed in service after December 31, 2024, the vehicle cannot include critical minerals extracted, processed, or recycled by a foreign entity of concern. [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(7)(A)]

The sources establish that to claim the clean vehicle credit under 26 U.S.C. § 30D(a), a vehicle must satisfy multiple requirements, including that it be a "new clean vehicle" meeting the definition in 26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1). That definition requires, among other things:

- Original use commences with the taxpayer [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(A)]
- Acquired for use or lease and not for resale [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(B)]

- Battery capacity of at least 7 kilowatt hours and capable of external recharge [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(F)]
- Final assembly in North America [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(G)]
- Proper reporting requirements met [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(1)(H)]

Additionally, for vehicles placed in service after December 31, 2023, components cannot be manufactured or assembled by a foreign entity of concern, and for those after December 31, 2024, critical minerals cannot be extracted, processed, or recycled by such an entity [26 U.S.C. § 30D(d)(7)].

answers.text:
Tax Year 2026

A heat pump may qualify for the energy efficient home improvement credit under 26 U.S.C. § 25C(a)(2), which allows a credit for "residential energy property expenditures" [26 U.S.C. § 25C(a)(2)]. 

Specifically, an "electric or natural gas heat pump" can be qualified energy property if it "meet[s] or exceed[s] the highest efficiency tier (not including any advanced tier) established by the Consortium for Energy Efficiency which is in effect as of the beginning of the calendar year in which the property is placed in service" [26 U.S.C. § 25C(d)(2)(A)(ii)].

For a heat pump installed in February 2026, the applicable efficiency standard is the Consortium for Energy Efficiency highest tier in effect at the beginning of 2026 [26 U.S.C. § 25C(d)(2)(A)(ii)].

**However, the sources do not specify which efficiency tier applies in 2026.** To determine eligibility, you must verify that the heat pump meets or exceeds the Consortium for Energy Efficiency's highest efficiency tier (not including any advanced tier) established for 2026.

If the heat pump qualifies, the credit is 30 percent of the expenditure, subject to a $2,000 annual limit on heat pumps [26 U.S.C. § 25C(a), (b)(5)].

INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.

The deduction for qualified overtime compensation under IRC section 225 is "applicable to taxable years beginning after Dec. 31, 2024" [26 U.S.C. § 225(a)-(f)]. answers.question: My client bought a new car for personal use in March 2024 with a loan secured by the car. Can she deduct the interest she pays on that loan in 2025 under the new car loan interest deduction?

answers.text:
**2025 Tax Year**

No, your client cannot deduct the interest under the qualified passenger vehicle loan interest deduction.

The qualified passenger vehicle loan interest deduction applies only to indebtedness "incurred by the taxpayer after December 31, 2024" [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(4)(B)(i)]. Because your client incurred the loan in March 2024, it does not meet this requirement. The statute is clear that only loans taken out after December 31, 2024 qualify for this deduction in 2025.

Additionally, the statute contains a related rule: a car first used for personal purposes cannot qualify for a section 179 deduction in a later year when its use changes to business [IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 22]. While this addresses a different deduction mechanism, it reflects the principle that personal-use property purchased before the 2025 tax year does not receive the new deductions created for 2025 forward.

answers.question: My client bought a new car for personal use in March 2024 with a loan secured by the car. Can she deduct the interest she pays on that loan in 2025 under the new car loan interest deduction?

answers.text:
**2025 Tax Year**

No, your client cannot deduct the interest under the new car loan interest deduction for qualified passenger vehicle loan interest.

To qualify for the deduction, the indebtedness must have been "incurred by the taxpayer after December 31, 2024" [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(4)(B)(i)]. Your client's loan was incurred in March 2024, which is before January 1, 2025, so it does not meet this requirement.

The qualified passenger vehicle loan interest deduction applies only to loans incurred after December 31, 2024, for taxable years 2025 through 2028 [26 U.S.C. § 163(h)(4)(A)].

**Tax year 2026**

No. Moving expenses are not deductible for tax year 2026.

Section 217(k)(1) suspends the deduction for moving expenses for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2017, except for members of the Armed Forces on active duty who move pursuant to a military order and incident to a permanent change of station, or employees or new appointees of the intelligence community (other than Armed Forces members) who move pursuant to a change in assignment requiring relocation. [26 U.S.C. § 217(k)(1)]

Unless the taxpayer falls into one of these exceptions, moving expenses are not deductible in 2026.

(a) Deduction allowed. There shall be allowed as a deduction moving expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in connection with the commencement of work by the taxpayer as an employee or as a self-employed individual at a new principal place of work.
(b) Definition of moving expenses. (1) In general. For purposes of this section, the term “moving expenses” means only the reasonable expenses— (A) of moving household goods and personal effects from the former residence to the new residence, and
(B) of traveling (including lodging) from the former residence to the new place of residence.
Such term shall not include any expenses for meals.
(2) Individuals other than taxpayer. In the case of any individual other than the taxpayer, expenses referred to in paragraph (1) shall be taken into account only if such individual has both the former residence and the new residence as his principal place of abode and is a member of the taxpayer’s household.

(B) if he had no former principal place of work, is at least 50 miles from his former residence, and
(2) either— (A) during the 12-month period immediately following his arrival in the general location of his new principal place of work, the taxpayer is a full-time employee, in such general location, during at least 39 weeks, or

For purposes of paragraph (1), the distance between two points shall be the shortest of the more commonly traveled routes between such two points.

No, moving expenses are not deductible for a taxpayer in 2026, with limited exceptions.

The deduction for moving expenses under section 217 is suspended for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017. [26 U.S.C. § 217(k)(1)]

For these excepted individuals, the moving expense deduction remains available. [26 U.S.C. § 217(g), (k)(2)]

Moving expenses are **not** deductible for 2026. [26 U.S.C. § 217(k)(1)]

**2026**

**Part 1: Statute of Limitations for Collection**

The IRS assessed your client's 2012 income tax on June 3, 2014. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6502(a)(1), such tax "may be collected by levy or by a proceeding in court" only "if the levy is made or the proceeding begun— within 10 years after the assessment of the tax." [26 U.S.C. § 6502(a)(1)]

Ten years from June 3, 2014 is June 3, 2024. In September 2026, more than ten years have elapsed since the assessment.

**Part 2: IRS Levy Authority After Expiration of Statute of Limitations**

Once the ten-year collection period under § 6502(a)(1) has expired, the IRS has no authority to levy. The statute provides no exception permitting levy after that period closes absent an installment agreement, court proceeding, or other triggering event. [26 U.S.C. § 6502(a)] Your client's facts exclude all such events.

**Conclusion**

No, the IRS cannot levy on your client's bank account in September 2026. The statute of limitations for collection expired on June 3, 2024.

DIEGO E. SALAZAR, Petitioner
v.
COMMISSIONER OF INTERNAL REVENUE, Respondent
__________
Docket No. 14285-23L.
Filed February 3, 2026.
__________
Hugh G. Jasne, for petitioner.
Gennady Zilberman, Rossana Gallego-Manzano, and Francesca Chou, for respondent.
MEMORANDUM OPINION
LAUBER, Judge: This collection due process (CDP) case relates to petitioner’s income tax liabilities for 2014–2017. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS or respondent) issued him a Notice of Determination sustaining a proposed levy, and he sought review in this Court. See § 6330(d)(1).1 Following a remand for a supplemental hearing, petitioner executed an installment agreement (IA) that resolved the tax liabilities in question. The IRS Independent Office of Appeals (Appeals) accordingly issued him a Supplemental Notice of Determination concluding that the levy, although appropriate when issued, would not be sustained because collection action was no longer necessary.
1 Unless otherwise indicated, statutory references are to the Internal Revenue Code, Title 26 U.S.C., in effect at all relevant times, regulation references are to the Code of Federal Regulations, Title 26 (Treas. Reg.), in effect at all relevant times, and Rule references are to the Tax Court Rules of Practice and Procedure. We round all monetary amounts to the nearest dollar.
Petitioner contends that he signed the IA “under protest,” desiring to maintain a challenge to the penalties and interest determined by the IRS for 2014–2017. Respondent has filed a Motion for Summary Judgment, contending that there are no disputes of material fact and that the settlement officer (SO) did not abuse her discretion in resolving the case as she did. We agree and accordingly will grant the Motion.
Background
contexts.heading: Diego E. Salazar v. Commissioner

contexts.text: 3 Petitioner appears to contend that his 2014–2017 liabilities were not timely assessed or that the period of limitations on collection had expired. Neither argument is correct. The IRS assessed the tax on August 12, 2019, shortly after petitioner failed to petition this Court. The assessments were thus timely under sections 6501(a) and 6503(a)(1) (providing that, after the mailing of a notice of deficiency, the running of the assessment period of limitations is suspended during the period in which the IRS is prohibited from making an assessment and for 60 days thereafter). The period of limitations on collection, which runs for 10 years after the date of assessment, § 6502(a)(1), has not yet expired. 4 Even if petitioner were entitled to challenge his liability for the penalties, he supplied during the CDP proceeding no evidence that the penalties were “excessive in amount,” were “erroneously or illegally assessed,” or were “attributable to erroneous written advice” from the IRS. See § 6404(a)(1), (3), (f) (authorizing abatement on these grounds). Instead, petitioner urged the SO to abate 50% of the penalties “out of fundamental fairness” on the theory that he had been victimized by an unscrupulous return preparer who had reported bogus deductions on his 2014–2017 returns. But taxpayers have a duty to review their returns for accuracy before the returns are filed, and the duty of filing accurate returns cannot be avoided by placing responsibility on a tax return preparer. See Metra Chem Corp. v. Commissioner, 88 T.C. 654, 662 (1987). Had petitioner discharged this duty, he would have seen (as he acknowledges in his Response) that the deductions were “significantly overreported.”

MEMORANDUM OPINION
LAUBER, Judge: This collection due process (CDP) case relates to petitioner’s income tax liabilities for 2014–2017. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS or respondent) issued him a Notice of Determination sustaining a proposed levy, and he sought review in this Court. See § 6330(d)(1).1 Following a remand for a supplemental hearing, petitioner executed an installment agreement (IA) that resolved the tax liabilities in question. The IRS Independent Office of Appeals (Appeals) accordingly issued him a Supplemental Notice of Determination concluding that the levy, although appropriate when issued, would not be sustained because collection action was no longer necessary.
1 Unless otherwise indicated, statutory references are to the Internal Revenue Code, Title 26 U.S.C., in effect at all relevant times, regulation references are to the Code of Federal Regulations, Title 26 (Treas. Reg.), in effect at all relevant times, and Rule references are to the Tax Court Rules of Practice and Procedure. We round all monetary amounts to the nearest dollar.
Petitioner contends that he signed the IA “under protest,” desiring to maintain a challenge to the penalties and interest determined by the IRS for 2014–2017. Respondent has filed a Motion for Summary Judgment, contending that there are no disputes of material fact and that the settlement officer (SO) did not abuse her discretion in resolving the case as she did. We agree and accordingly will grant the Motion.
Background
contexts.heading: Diego E. Salazar v. Commissioner

contexts.text: 3 Petitioner appears to contend that his 2014–2017 liabilities were not timely assessed or that the period of limitations on collection had expired. Neither argument is correct. The IRS assessed the tax on August 12, 2019, shortly after petitioner failed to petition this Court. The assessments were thus timely under sections 6501(a) and 6503(a)(1) (providing that, after the mailing of a notice of deficiency, the running of the assessment period of limitations is suspended during the period in which the IRS is prohibited from making an assessment and for 60 days thereafter). The period of limitations on collection, which runs for 10 years after the date of assessment, § 6502(a)(1), has not yet expired. 4 Even if petitioner were entitled to challenge his liability for the penalties, he supplied during the CDP proceeding no evidence that the penalties were “excessive in amount,” were “erroneously or illegally assessed,” or were “attributable to erroneous written advice” from the IRS. See § 6404(a)(1), (3), (f) (authorizing abatement on these grounds). Instead, petitioner urged the SO to abate 50% of the penalties “out of fundamental fairness” on the theory that he had been victimized by an unscrupulous return preparer who had reported bogus deductions on his 2014–2017 returns. But taxpayers have a duty to review their returns for accuracy before the returns are filed, and the duty of filing accurate returns cannot be avoided by placing responsibility on a tax return preparer. See Metra Chem Corp. v. Commissioner, 88 T.C. 654, 662 (1987). Had petitioner discharged this duty, he would have seen (as he acknowledges in his Response) that the deductions were “significantly overreported.”

answers.text:
**Tax Year 2026**

No. The IRS cannot levy on your client's bank account in September 2026.

The statute of limitations for collection of federal income tax expires 10 years after assessment. [26 U.S.C. § 6502(a)(1)] Your client's 2012 income tax was assessed on June 3, 2014, so the collection period expires on June 3, 2024. [26 U.S.C. § 6502(a)(1)] Since there has been no installment agreement, levy, court proceeding, or suspension of the limitations period, the 10-year period has run without interruption. [26 U.S.C. § 6502(a), § 6503] By September 2026, the IRS has lost authority to collect by levy.

answers.question: My single client had adjusted gross income of $60,000 in 2023 and paid $3,000 of day care for her 6-year-old so she could work. What percentage of those expenses did her child and dependent care credit cover for 2023?

answers.text:
# 2026 Tax Year

The applicable percentage for the child and dependent care credit is determined by your client's adjusted gross income under a formula that reduces a base percentage.

The base percentage is 50 percent. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)] This is reduced by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 (or fraction thereof) by which adjusted gross income exceeds $15,000, but not below 35 percent. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)(A)] It is further reduced by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 by which adjusted gross income exceeds $75,000, but not below 20 percent. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)(B)]

With adjusted gross income of $60,000:
- The excess over $15,000 is $45,000, which is 22.5 times $2,000, requiring a reduction of 22 percentage points (rounding the fraction up), bringing the percentage to 28 percent.
- The AGI does not exceed $75,000, so the second reduction does not apply.

The applicable percentage is therefore **28 percent**. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)]

answers.question: My single client has adjusted gross income of $60,000 and is paying $3,000 of day care this year for her 6-year-old so she can work. What percentage of those expenses will her child and dependent care credit cover on this year's return?

answers.text:
**2026**

Part 1: Percentage of qualifying expenses for the child and dependent care credit based on adjusted gross income

The applicable percentage for the dependent care credit starts at 50 percent and is reduced by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 (or fraction thereof) by which the taxpayer's adjusted gross income exceeds $15,000, but not below 35 percent. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)(A)]

Your client's AGI of $60,000 exceeds $15,000 by $45,000. Dividing $45,000 by $2,000 equals 22.5, which rounds up to 23 percentage points of reduction. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)(A)]

Starting from 50 percent and reducing by 23 percentage points yields 27 percent. However, the reduction cannot go below 35 percent. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)(A)]

Therefore, the applicable percentage is **35 percent**, which means the credit will cover 35 percent of the $3,000 in qualifying expenses, or $1,050.

answers.text:
**Tax year: 2026**

For your client's dependent care credit, the applicable percentage is determined by her adjusted gross income under a two-step reduction formula. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)]

The applicable percentage starts at 50 percent, reduced (but not below 35 percent) by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 or fraction thereof by which AGI exceeds $15,000, and further reduced (but not below 20 percent) by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 by which AGI exceeds $75,000. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)]

With AGI of $60,000:
- First reduction: ($60,000 − $15,000) = $45,000 ÷ $2,000 = 22.5, rounded up to 23 percentage points. 50% − 23% = 27%.
- Second reduction does not apply since $60,000 does not exceed $75,000.
- Result: 27%, but this cannot fall below 20 percent, so the applicable percentage is **27 percent**. [26 U.S.C. § 21(a)(2)]

The credit covers 27% of the $3,000 in employment-related expenses, or $810.

answers.text:
**Tax year 2022:**

Your client can take the $6,000 deduction for seniors on her 2022 return. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017 and before January 1, 2029, there is allowed a deduction of $6,000 for each qualified individual, which includes a taxpayer who has attained age 65 before the close of the taxable year. [26 U.S.C. § 151(d)(5)(C)(i)-(ii)] Since your client turned 70 in 2020, she had attained age 65 before the close of 2022 and qualifies for this deduction.

**Tax year 2029:**

Your client will not be able to take this deduction on her 2029 return. The $6,000 deduction for seniors applies only to taxable years beginning before January 1, 2029. [26 U.S.C. § 151(d)(5)(C)(i)] Since 2029 is a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028, she is not eligible for this deduction in that year.

Most taxpayers have a choice of either taking a standard deduction or itemizing their deductions. If you have a choice, you can use the method that gives you the lower tax. (e) Vehicle cents-per-mile valuation rule —(1) In general —(i) General rule. Under the vehicle cents-per-mile valuation rule of this paragraph (e), if an employer provides an employee with the use of a vehicle that—
(A) The employer reasonably expects will be regularly used in the employer's trade or business throughout the calendar year (or such shorter period as the vehicle may be owned or leased by the employer), or
(B) Satisfies the requirements of paragraph (e)(1)(ii) of this section, the value of the benefit provided in the calendar year is the standard mileage rate provided in the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure (“cents-per-mile rate”) multiplied by the total number of miles the vehicle is driven by the employee for personal purposes. The cents-per-mile rate is to be applied prospectively from the first day of the taxable year following the date of publication of the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure. An employee who uses an employer-provided vehicle, in whole or in part, for a trade or business other than the employer's trade or business, may take a deduction for such business use based upon the vehicle cents-per-mile rule as long as such deduction is at the same standard mileage rate as that used in calculating the employee's income inclusion. The standard mileage rate must be applied to personal miles independent of business miles. Thus, for example, if the standard mileage rate were 24 cents per mile for the first 15,000 miles and 11 cents per mile for all miles over 15,000 and an employee drives 20,000 personal miles and 45,000 business miles in a year, the value of the personal use of the vehicle is $4,150 ((15,000 × $.24) + (5,000 × $.11)). The cents-per-mile rate is to be applied prospectively from the first day of the taxable year following the date of publication of the applicable Revenue Ruling or Revenue Procedure. An employee who uses an employer-provided vehicle, in whole or in part, for a trade or business other than the employer's trade or business, may take a deduction for such business use based upon the vehicle cents-per-mile rule as long as such deduction is at the same standard mileage rate as that used in calculating the employee's income inclusion. # Part 1: Whether Burden Shifting Decides a Hobby Loss Case

No. Even if your client meets the section 7491(a) requirements and the burden shifts to the IRS, that will not necessarily decide the case.

In a hobby loss case, the Tax Court may decide the case on the preponderance of the evidence without applying section 7491 at all. [T.C. Memo. 2023-87, at *11-12]. The Court stated: "the outcome of this case is based on a preponderance of the evidence and thus is unaffected by section 7491." [T.C. Memo. 2023-87, at *11-12]. Similarly, in another case, the Court explained: "we need not decide which party bears the burden of proof for such issues" because it could "decide most issues on the basis of the preponderance of the evidence." [T.C. Memo. 2026-51, at *9-10].

Therefore, even with burden shifting in your client's favor under section 7491(a), the Tax Court may simply find the facts one way or the other under the preponderance standard, making the burden-shifting provision irrelevant to the outcome.

(b) Use of statistical information on unrelated taxpayers. In the case of an individual taxpayer, the Secretary shall have the burden of proof in any court proceeding with respect to any item of income which was reconstructed by the Secretary solely through the use of statistical information on unrelated taxpayers.

# Tax Court Alternative Arguments Raised for the First Time in Post-Trial Briefs

A taxpayer may win on an alternative argument raised for the first time in a post-trial brief, but only under limited circumstances.

**General Rule:** Tax Court will not consider issues first raised in parties' briefs where prejudice and surprise are found to exist. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *13-14]

**Exception:** Tax Court may consider an alternative argument raised for the first time on brief if:

1. **The argument appeals to the correct application of the law** based on the same legal provisions the parties have relied upon from the outset, rather than invoking new or elective statutory provisions for the first time; [116 T.C. No. 29, at *12-13]

2. **The record contains sufficient facts** to permit the Court to decide the case on the grounds of the alternative argument, with neither party suggesting the record is insufficient; [116 T.C. No. 29, at *12-13]

3. **Prejudice to the opposing party is minimal or absent.** For example, if the alternative argument does not require presentation of different evidence and the Commissioner can adequately respond based on the existing record, prejudice may not preclude consideration. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *9-10, *12-13]

By contrast, Tax Court will reject alternative arguments raised on brief where they rely on elective or new statutory provisions or create unfair prejudice through timing (such as raising arguments after assessment periods expire). [116 T.C. No. 29, at *13-14]

answers.text:
# Answer

A taxpayer **can** win in Tax Court on an alternative argument raised for the first time in a post-trial brief, but only under narrow circumstances where prejudice and surprise are not found to exist.

The general rule is that Tax Court will **not** consider issues first raised in parties' briefs where prejudice and surprise are found to exist. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *13-14]

However, the Court will consider a late-raised alternative argument if:

1. **The argument appeals to the correct application of law** based on the same legal provisions that were at issue from the outset, rather than invoking new or elective statutory provisions for the first time. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *12-13]

2. **The record is sufficient** to permit the Court to dispose of the case on the grounds of the alternative argument, with neither party suggesting that insufficient facts exist. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *12-13]

3. **No special prejudice exists** to the opposing party, such as the expiration of the statute of limitations shortly before the brief was filed. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *9-10]

By contrast, a taxpayer will **not** prevail if the alternative argument is based on elective statutory provisions invoked for the first time on brief. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *13-14]

Additionally, issues raised for the first time only in an **answering brief** (rather than opening brief) may be abandoned and conceded. [T.C. Memo. 2026-51, at *11]

answers.question: Can a taxpayer win in Tax Court on an alternative argument raised for the first time in its post-trial brief?

answers.text:
# Answer

A taxpayer can win on an alternative argument raised for the first time in a post-trial brief, but only in narrow circumstances where the court finds no prejudice or surprise to the opposing party and the argument appeals to the correct application of law already in issue.

## General Rule Against Late-Raised Arguments

Tax Court will not consider issues first raised in parties' briefs where prejudice and surprise exist. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *13-14]

## Exception: When Alternative Arguments May Be Considered

An alternative argument raised for the first time on brief may be considered if:

1. **No prejudice exists**: The argument must not prejudice the opposing party. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *13-14]

2. **The argument appeals to correct application of law already in issue**: The argument must be based on the same legal provisions the parties have litigated from the outset, not on new elective statutory provisions invoked for the first time on brief. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *12-13]

3. **The record is sufficient**: Neither party has suggested the record contains insufficient facts to dispose of the case on the alternative argument's grounds. [116 T.C. No. 29, at *12-13]

## Contrasting Example

Tax Court rejected an alternative argument raised for the first time on brief where it was "predicated on other elective statutory provisions invoked for the first time on brief" and did not "necessarily appeal to the correct application of the law." [116 T.C. No. 29, at *13-14]

Additionally, Tax Court may treat an issue raised for the first time in an answering brief as abandoned and conceded. [T.C. Memo. 2026-51, at *11]

As germane here, each of these cases stands for the general proposition that this Court will not consider issues first raised in the parties’ briefs where prejudice and surprise are found to exist. **Tax year 2026**

Yes, the Tax Court can review the IRS's refusal to allow participation in the Voluntary Classification Settlement Program.

The Tax Court has jurisdiction under section 7436(a) to determine "the proper amounts of employment taxes which relate to the Commissioner's determination concerning worker classification." [158 T.C. No. 6, at *2-4] This jurisdiction includes the ability to review whether the VCSP applies to the computation of employment tax liability. [158 T.C. No. 6, at *1-2] The Tax Court rejected the IRS's argument that it lacked jurisdiction to review the VCSP denial in an employment tax case. [158 T.C. No. 6, at *2-4]

To participate in the VCSP, a taxpayer must: (1) have consistently treated the workers as nonemployees; (2) have filed all required Forms 1099, consistent with the nonemployee treatment, for the previous three years; and (3) not currently be under employment tax audit by the IRS. [T.C. Memo. 2022-38, at *3] The IRS may deny participation only if the taxpayer does not meet these eligibility requirements. [T.C. Memo. 2022-38, at *3]

(a) Authority of Secretary. If any person liable to pay any tax neglects or refuses to pay the same within 10 days after notice and demand, it shall be lawful for the Secretary to collect such tax (and such further sum as shall be sufficient to cover the expenses of the levy) by levy upon all property and rights to property (except such property as is exempt under section 6334) belonging to such person or on which there is a lien provided in this chapter for the payment of such tax. Levy may be made upon the accrued salary or wages of any officer, employee, or elected official, of the United States, the District of Columbia, or any agency or instrumentality of the United States or the District of Columbia, by serving a notice of levy on the employer (as defined in section 3401(d)) of such officer, employee, or elected official. If the Secretary makes a finding that the collection of such tax is in jeopardy, notice and demand for immediate payment of such tax may be made by the Secretary and, upon failure or refusal to pay such tax, collection thereof by levy shall be lawful without regard to the 10-day period provided in this section.
(b) Seizure and sale of property. The term “levy” as used in this title includes the power of distraint and seizure by any means. Except as otherwise provided in subsection (e), a levy shall extend only to property possessed and obligations existing at the time thereof. In any case in which the Secretary may levy upon property or rights to property, he may seize and sell such property or rights to property (whether real or personal, tangible or intangible).
(c) Successive seizures. Whenever any property or right to property upon which levy has been made by virtue of subsection (a) is not sufficient to satisfy the claim of the United States for which levy is made, the Secretary may, thereafter, and as often as may be necessary, proceed to levy in like manner upon any other property liable to levy of the person against whom such claim exists, until the amount due from him, together with all expenses, is fully paid.

answers.question: The IRS reclassified my client's corporate officer as an employee and refused to let the company pay under the Voluntary Classification Settlement Program. Can the Tax Court review that refusal?

answers.text:
**2026**

**Part 1: Tax Court Jurisdiction Over IRS Refusal to Allow VCSP**

Yes. The Tax Court has jurisdiction to review the IRS's determination that the VCSP does not apply to the computation of your client's employment tax liability.

The Tax Court has jurisdiction under section 7436(a) to determine "the proper amounts of employment taxes which relate to the Commissioner's determination concerning worker classification." [T.C. Memo. 2022-38, at *3] The IRS's refusal to allow VCSP participation directly affects the proper amount of employment taxes owed, which falls within this jurisdiction. [158 T.C. No. 6, at *2] Specifically, in *Treece Financial Services Group v. Commissioner*, the Tax Court held that "the Tax Court has jurisdiction in this employment tax case to determine whether respondent's determination that the VCSP does not apply to the computation of petitioner's employment tax liability is correct," rejecting the IRS's argument that the Court lacked jurisdiction to review the VCSP denial. [158 T.C. No. 6, at *1-2]

If any person liable to pay any tax neglects or refuses to pay the same within 10 days after notice and demand, it shall be lawful for the Secretary to collect such tax (and such further sum as shall be sufficient to cover the expenses of the levy) by levy upon all property and rights to property (except such property as is exempt under section 6334) belonging to such person or on which there is a lien provided in this chapter for the payment of such tax. The VCSP provides partial relief from federal employment taxes for eligible taxpayers that agree to treat workers prospectively as employees. I.R.S. Announcement 2012-45, 2012-51 I.R.B. 724, 724. To be eligible for the VCSP, a taxpayer must: (1) have consistently treated the workers as nonemployees; (2) have filed all required Forms 1099, consistent with the nonemployee treatment, for the previous three years; and (3) not currently be under employment tax audit by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Id. Petitioner submitted Form 8952, Application for Voluntary Classification Settlement Program (VCSP), on October 23, 2018. Respondent denied petitioner participation in the VCSP on February 28, 2019, stating: “You’re under an employment tax examination by the IRS.”
Discussion
We will first decide respondent’s Motion to Partially Dismiss. If we determine that we have jurisdiction, we will then address petitioner’s Motion for Summary Judgment.
I.
Respondent’s Motion to Partially Dismiss
The Tax Court may exercise jurisdiction only to the extent expressly provided by Congress. See § 7442; Breman v. Commissioner, 66 T.C. 61, 66 (1976). We, however, have the authority to determine whether we have jurisdiction over a particular case. Kluger v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 309, 314 (1984). Generally, we have jurisdiction under section 7436(a) to determine: (1) whether an individual providing services to a person is that person’s employee for purposes of subtitle C; (2) whether the person, if an employer, is entitled to relief under section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978; and (3) the proper amounts of employment taxes which relate to the Commissioner’s determination concerning worker classification.
